The auxiliary みる is metaphorically related to 見る ('see') — you do the action and 'see' how it turns out — but is written in hiragana to distinguish from the literal sense of seeing. The past form みた reports the outcome of the trial.
formation: Vて + みる (polite: みます). Always in hiragana when used as this auxiliary; do not write 見る.

examples.ja: 新しい料理を作ってみた。
examples.en: I tried making a new dish.

examples.ja: このくつを履いてみてもいいですか。
examples.en: May I try on these shoes?

examples.ja: 一度日本に行ってみたい。
examples.en: I want to try going to Japan once.

meaning_en: going on / away from reference point (spatially or temporally)
meaning_detailed: Vて + いく expresses movement or progression away from a reference point — usually the speaker's current position in space or time. Spatially, this is action moving away ('run off', 'walk away'). Temporally, it is gradual change continuing into the future from now ('will continue to X', 'will become more X'). Contrast with 〜てくる, which is the opposite direction.
formation: Vて + いく (polite: いきます). Can be written 行く or いく; the auxiliary use is more commonly in hiragana.

examples.ja: 子供たちは元気に学校へ走っていった。
examples.en: The children ran off to school full of energy.

examples.ja: 季節が変わっていく。
examples.en: The seasons are changing (progressively).

examples.ja: これからも日本語を勉強していきます。
examples.en: I will continue studying Japanese from now on.

meaning_en: coming to / becoming (toward reference point)
meaning_detailed: Vて + くる expresses movement or progression toward a reference point — usually the speaker's current position in space or time. Spatially, action moves toward the speaker ('come running'). Temporally, it expresses gradual change from the past up to now ('has come to X', 'has been becoming X'). Also used for 'go and come back' — a round-trip sense that is very common in everyday speech.
formation: Vて + くる (polite: きます). Can be written 来る or くる; the auxiliary use is more commonly in hiragana.

examples.ja: 彼が駅から走ってきた。
examples.en: He came running from the station.

examples.ja: だんだん暖かくなってきました。
examples.en: It has been gradually warming up.

examples.ja: ちょっとパンを買ってきます。
examples.en: I'll go get some bread (and come back).

pattern: V 〜ている / noun-の / adj + 間 or 間に
meaning_en: during / while (a period within which something happens)
meaning_detailed: 〜間 and 〜間に both express temporal 'during / while', but differ in scope: 〜間 (without に) covers the whole duration and is used with continuous main-clause actions that also span the whole period. 〜間に (with に) marks a point or sub-interval within the period, and is used for one-off events that happen during it. Subjects in the main clause and the 間 clause can differ.
formation: Noun + の + 間(に); V 〜ている + 間(に); V plain + 間(に); i-adj + 間(に); na-adj + な + 間(に).

examples.ja: 私が留守の間に誰か来ましたか。
examples.en: Did someone come while I was out?

examples.ja: 夏休みの間、ずっと旅行していました。
examples.en: I was traveling the whole time during summer vacation.

examples.ja: 母が料理している間に、宿題をした。
examples.en: While my mother was cooking, I did my homework.

meaning_en: just (now) did / just about to do / in the middle of doing
meaning_detailed: ところ combined with different verb forms expresses the aspectual 'point of doing' an action: Vる + ところ = 'just about to', V 〜ている + ところ = 'in the middle of', Vた + ところ = 'just did (right now)'. Unlike 〜たばかり (subjective recency), 〜たところ refers to the immediate, clock-objective moment.
formation: V plain non-past + ところ (about to); V 〜ている + ところ (in the middle); V plain past + ところ (just did). All optionally followed by だ/です.

examples.ja: 今、駅に着いたところです。
examples.en: I just arrived at the station (right now).

examples.ja: ちょうどご飯を食べているところです。
examples.en: I'm in the middle of eating right now.

examples.ja: 今から出かけるところだ。
examples.en: I'm just about to go out.

pattern: V plain / noun-の + おかげで (positive) or せいで (negative)
meaning_en: thanks to / because of (with explicit positive or negative attribution)
meaning_detailed: おかげで and せいで both attribute a result to a cause, but with opposite polarity: おかげで ('thanks to') is used for positive outcomes, while せいで ('because of / at the fault of') is used for negative outcomes. They are structural twins — same connection patterns, opposite valence — and are typically taught as a pair.
formation: V plain / i-adj + おかげで / せいで. Na-adj + な + おかげで / せいで. Noun + の + おかげで / せいで. Past forms also allowed: 手伝ってくれたおかげで, 雨が降ったせいで.

examples.ja: あなたのおかげで合格できました。
examples.en: Thanks to you, I was able to pass.

examples.ja: 彼のせいで試合に負けた。
examples.en: We lost the match because of him.

examples.ja: 雨のせいで遅れました。
examples.en: I was late because of the rain.

meaning_en: half-done / in the middle of / about to (interrupted action)
meaning_detailed: V ます-stem + かける attaches to a verb to express that an action has been started but not completed — 'half-doing', 'about to do', or 'partway through'. The attributive form 〜かけの + noun is also productive ('a half-X thing'). With some verbs it takes on the sense 'on the verge of' (死にかける 'nearly die').
formation: V ます-stem + かける (polite: かけます). Attributive form for nouns: 〜かけの + N (食べかけのケーキ 'half-eaten cake').

examples.ja: 読みかけの本が机の上にある。
examples.en: There's a book I haven't finished on the desk.

examples.ja: ケーキを食べかけたところで電話が鳴った。
examples.en: Just as I started eating the cake, the phone rang.

examples.ja: 彼は何か言いかけてやめた。
examples.en: He started to say something but stopped.

pattern: Noun / verb plain + ほど; also A は B ほど [adj]-ない
meaning_en: to the extent of / not as ___ as
meaning_detailed: ほど expresses degree or extent — either hyperbolically ('tired to death' = 死ぬほど疲れた) or comparatively in the negative construction A は B ほど [adj]-ない ('A is not as ___ as B'). In comparisons, ほど marks the reference against which A falls short. Hyperbolic phrases like 山ほど ('a mountain of') and 死ぬほど ('to death') are highly productive.
formation: Noun / V plain + ほど. Negative comparison: A は B ほど + adjective-ない. Modifier form: 〜ほどの + N.

examples.ja: 今日は死ぬほど疲れた。
examples.en: I'm dead tired today.

examples.ja: 東京は大阪ほど暑くない。
examples.en: Tokyo isn't as hot as Osaka.

examples.ja: 彼ほど日本語が上手な外国人は少ない。
examples.en: There are few foreigners as good at Japanese as him.

pattern: Noun / verb plain + くらい / ぐらい
meaning_en: about / approximately / to the extent that
meaning_detailed: くらい (voiced variant ぐらい; both interchangeable) expresses approximate quantity ('about X') or degree ('to the extent that'). For numbers, it is the most common way to say 'approximately'. For degree of emotion or state, it is used hyperbolically like ほど, but with a more casual register. It also has a minimizing sense: 'at least that much' (それくらいは... expected).
formation: Number/quantity + くらい/ぐらい: 10分くらい ('about 10 minutes'). V plain + くらい: 泣きたいくらい嬉しい ('so happy I could cry'). Noun + くらい: これくらい.

examples.ja: 駅まで歩いて20分くらいかかります。
examples.en: It takes about 20 minutes to walk to the station.

examples.ja: 泣きたいくらい嬉しかった。
examples.en: I was so happy I could have cried.

examples.ja: それくらい自分でやってください。
examples.en: At least do that much yourself.

pattern: Verb plain form / na-adj + な + こと
meaning_en: nominalizer: 'the act / fact of doing'
meaning_detailed: こと turns a verb or adjective phrase into a noun, expressing 'the act of doing' or 'the fact that'. It is used for abstract, general, or factual statements — in contrast to の-nominalization, which is used for more concrete / perceptual situations. Several fixed grammar patterns require こと specifically (〜ことができる, 〜ことにする, 〜ことになる, 〜ことがある).
formation: V plain + こと (食べること, 勉強したこと). Na-adj + な + こと (静かなこと, 元気なこと). i-adj + こと (高いこと).

examples.ja: 日本語を勉強することは楽しいです。
examples.en: Studying Japanese is fun.

examples.ja: 彼が来ないことを知らなかった。
examples.en: I didn't know that he wasn't coming.

examples.ja: 早く起きることは大切だ。
examples.en: Rising early is important.

pattern: Verb plain form / na-adj + な + の
meaning_en: nominalizer: 'the act / fact of doing' (perceptual/concrete)
meaning_detailed: の turns a verb or adjective phrase into a noun, used for concrete, perceptual, or immediate situations — 'I saw him running' (走るのを見た). With perception verbs (見る, 聞く, 感じる), の is strongly preferred over こと. In more abstract or factual contexts, こと is preferred. Both are nominalizers, but their register and context of use differ.
formation: V plain + の (走るの, 食べるの). Na-adj + な + の (静かなの). i-adj + の (高いの).

examples.ja: 彼が走るのを見た。
examples.en: I saw him running.

examples.ja: 雨が降っているのが聞こえる。
examples.en: I can hear the rain falling.

examples.ja: 絵を描くのが好きです。
examples.en: I like drawing pictures.

meaning_en: by means of / depending on / by (passive agent)
meaning_detailed: によって has three related senses: (1) means / method — 'by means of', more formal than で; (2) variation — 'depending on' (意見は人によって違う 'opinions differ by person'); (3) passive agent — marking who performed an action in passive sentences, especially in formal or written contexts. The form によっては emphasizes variability.
formation: Noun + によって (adverbially). Noun + による + noun (attributively): 〜による研究. Variation emphasis: によっては.

examples.ja: 意見は人によって違う。
examples.en: Opinions differ depending on the person.

examples.ja: この問題は話し合いによって解決した。
examples.en: We resolved this problem through discussion.

examples.ja: この絵はピカソによって描かれた。
examples.en: This painting was painted by Picasso.

pattern: Verb-た form + ほうがいい
meaning_en: had better / it's better to
meaning_detailed: 〜たほうがいい expresses advice or recommendation — 'you'd better do X'. Counterintuitively, the affirmative form uses Vた (which looks like past tense but here functions as a fixed construction). The negative form uses V ない. Softer than べきだ (moral should) and more common in everyday speech for giving advice.
formation: Vた + ほうがいい (affirmative). V ない + ほうがいい (negative). Polite: ほうがいいです. Past: ほうがよかった ('should have').

examples.ja: 早く寝たほうがいいよ。
examples.en: You'd better go to bed early.

examples.ja: 医者に行ったほうがいいです。
examples.en: You should go to the doctor.

examples.ja: あんまり食べないほうがいい。
examples.en: You'd better not eat too much.

pattern: Verb-ない stem + なくちゃ / なきゃ (+ いけない / ならない)
meaning_en: must / have to (casual contractions)
meaning_detailed: なくちゃ and なきゃ are casual contractions of the formal 〜なくてはいけない / 〜なければならない ('must do'). In everyday speech, the trailing いけない / ならない is often dropped entirely, leaving just なくちゃ / なきゃ at sentence-final position. Register is strictly casual; avoid in polite or formal contexts.
formation: V ない-form → replace ない with: なくちゃ (from 〜なくては) or なきゃ (from 〜なければ). Examples: 食べなくちゃ / 食べなきゃ, 行かなくちゃ / 行かなきゃ. Optional trailing いけない / ならない in less casual usage.

examples.ja: もう帰らなきゃ。
examples.en: I have to go home now.

examples.ja: 明日までに宿題をやらなくちゃ。
examples.en: I have to do my homework by tomorrow.

examples.ja: 早く起きなきゃいけない。
examples.en: I have to get up early.

fullKey: verb-ないstem+なくちゃなきゃ+いけないならない

meaning_en: should have / would have been better if
meaning_detailed: 〜ばよかった expresses regret about a past action (or inaction) — 'I should have done X' or 'it would have been better if X had happened'. The structure is literally 'if (ば form) it had been good (よかった)'. The negative form 〜なければよかった means 'I shouldn't have done X'. Often paired with のに for emphasis.
formation: V ば-form + よかった: 行けばよかった ('should have gone'). Negative: V なければ + よかった: 言わなければよかった ('shouldn't have said'). Adjectives and nouns can also take the construction via their ば-forms.

examples.ja: もっと勉強すればよかった。
examples.en: I should have studied more.

examples.ja: あの時買っておけばよかった。
examples.en: I should have bought it then.

examples.ja: そんなこと、言わなければよかった。
examples.en: I shouldn't have said such a thing.

meaning_en: be made to do / be forced to do
meaning_detailed: The causative-passive combines the causative and passive — literally 'be made to do by someone'. It almost always implies unwilling compulsion: the subject is a reluctant performer of the action. Structurally it chains the causative (させる / せる) and passive (られる) auxiliaries, with a common contracted form for godan verbs that is very frequent in speech.
formation: Ichidan: drop る, add させられる (食べる → 食べさせられる). Godan: u-row → a-row + せられる, OR contracted u-row → a-row + される (except 〜す verbs, which do not contract). Irregular: する → させられる, くる → こさせられる.

examples.ja: 私は母に野菜を食べさせられた。
examples.en: I was made to eat vegetables by my mother.

examples.ja: 先生に1時間待たされた。
examples.en: I was made to wait for an hour by the teacher.

examples.ja: 毎日宿題をさせられる。
examples.en: I'm made to do homework every day.

pattern: Verb stem + たがる / たがっている
meaning_en: (third person) wants to / shows signs of wanting
meaning_detailed: たがる expresses that a third person wants to do something — where Japanese treats one's own desires (〜たい) and others' desires differently. Others' inner states are observable only through behavior, so 〜たがる literally frames it as 'show signs of wanting'. Often used with children, pets, or people whose desires the speaker is inferring from their actions.
formation: V ます-stem + たがる: 食べたがる, 行きたがる. Conjugates as a godan u-verb: 食べたがります, 食べたがらない, 食べたがった. Progressive form for current desire: たがっている (most common in modern usage).

examples.ja: 子供は甘いものを食べたがる。
examples.en: Children want to eat sweet things.

examples.ja: 彼は行きたがっているようだ。
examples.en: It seems he wants to go.

examples.ja: 妹は新しい服を買いたがっている。
examples.en: My little sister wants to buy new clothes.

pattern: Noun + さえ (+ negative or extreme statement)
meaning_en: even (emphatic, minimal case)
meaning_detailed: さえ is an emphatic particle meaning 'even' — it highlights a minimal or unexpected case to make a point, often 'if even X (which is basic/minimal), then surely Y'. Commonly paired with conditional constructions (さえ〜ば 'if only X') or with negative statements to express surprise or disbelief ('even X doesn't Y'). More emphatic than でも in this sense.
formation: Noun + さえ (+ predicate). Also: V ます-stem + さえすれば ('if only one does X'); Noun + さえ + conditional.

examples.ja: 子供さえ知っている。
examples.en: Even a child knows.

examples.ja: お金さえあれば、買えるのに。
examples.en: If only I had money, I could buy it.

examples.ja: 彼は名前さえ書けなかった。
examples.en: He couldn't even write his name.

meaning_en: the moment that / as soon as
meaning_detailed: 〜たとたん(に) expresses that the main-clause event happens IMMEDIATELY and unexpectedly at the completion of the 〜た form event. Often conveys surprise or a sudden transition. Distinct from 〜たらすぐ ('as soon as', more neutral) — とたん has a stronger sense of instantaneous, often surprising, simultaneity.
formation: V-た + とたん(に).

examples.ja: ドアを開けたとたん、猫が飛び出した。
examples.en: The moment I opened the door, the cat jumped out.

examples.ja: 家に着いたとたんに、雨が降り始めた。
examples.en: Just as I got home, it started raining.

examples.ja: 彼の顔を見たとたん、昔を思い出した。
examples.en: The moment I saw his face, I remembered the past.

pattern: V plain / i-adj / noun + である + 限り
meaning_en: as long as / to the extent that / as far as
meaning_detailed: 〜限り has several related senses: (1) 'as long as' (as a condition continues) — V plain non-past + 限り; (2) 'to the extent that / as far as' (limit of knowledge or ability) — 知っている限り ('as far as I know'); (3) 'as long as X is the case' (condition on a state). A versatile marker for expressing scope or limit.
formation: V plain non-past + 限り; i-adj + 限り; noun + である + 限り; na-adj + な + 限り. Negative: V ない + 限り ('unless').

examples.ja: 生きている限り、希望はある。
examples.en: As long as you're alive, there's hope.

examples.ja: 知っている限り、教えてあげる。
examples.en: I'll tell you as much as I know.

examples.ja: 努力しない限り、成功できない。
examples.en: Unless you make an effort, you can't succeed.

pattern: Plain form + わけではない
meaning_en: it's not (necessarily) that / it doesn't mean that
meaning_detailed: 〜わけではない softens a negative — 'it's not that I don't X' or 'that doesn't mean X'. It hedges an implication that the speaker wants to deny without outright rejecting the broader topic. Common in explanations when correcting a listener's assumption: 'it's not like I hate it, it's just that...'. The casual contracted form is わけじゃない.
formation: V plain / i-adj + わけではない / わけじゃない; na-adj + な + わけではない; noun + という + わけではない.

examples.ja: 嫌いなわけじゃないけど、今日は食べたくない。
examples.en: It's not that I dislike it, I just don't feel like eating it today.

examples.ja: 毎日忙しいわけではない。
examples.en: I'm not necessarily busy every day.

examples.ja: 日本語が話せないわけじゃない。
examples.en: It's not that I can't speak Japanese.

pattern: Verb ます-stem + ようがない / ようもない
meaning_en: there's no way to / can't possibly
meaning_detailed: 〜ようがない expresses that there is no method, no way, or no possibility to do something — 'it's impossible to X'. Attached to the verb's ます-stem. The intensive form 〜ようもない is slightly stronger. Distinct from 〜できない (simple 'cannot') in that 〜ようがない emphasizes the absence of any method, not just the lack of ability.
formation: V ます-stem + ようがない / ようもない.

examples.ja: 電話番号が分からないから、連絡のしようがない。
examples.en: I don't know his number, so there's no way to contact him.

examples.ja: この気持ちは言いようがない。
examples.en: There's no way to describe this feeling.

examples.ja: 壊れてしまって、直しようがない。
examples.en: It's broken and there's no way to fix it.

key: ようがないようもない
fullKey: verbます-stem+ようがないようもない

meaning_en: ever since / since (a specific past event)
meaning_detailed: 〜以来 marks a past time point as the starting anchor for an ongoing state or repeated action — 'ever since X'. Attaches to the て-form of verbs or directly to nouns. Distinct from 〜てから (neutral 'after') in that 以来 emphasizes continuous or repeated effect from the past point up to now. Formal / written register.
formation: V-て + 以来; noun + 以来.

examples.ja: 日本に来て以来、毎日日本語を勉強している。
examples.en: Ever since I came to Japan, I've been studying Japanese every day.

examples.ja: 卒業以来、彼に会っていない。
examples.en: I haven't seen him since graduation.

examples.ja: あの事件以来、彼は人を信じられなくなった。
examples.en: Ever since that incident, he hasn't been able to trust people.

pattern: Noun + に関して / に関する
meaning_en: regarding / concerning (formal)
meaning_detailed: 〜に関して is a more formal variant of について ('about / regarding'). Common in business, academic writing, news, and formal speech. The attributive form に関する + noun is productive in titles and headlines. Functionally close to について but with a more formal, topical feel.
formation: Noun + に関して (adverbially). Noun + に関する + noun (attributively).

examples.ja: この問題に関して、意見がありますか。
examples.en: Do you have any opinions regarding this issue?

examples.ja: 環境問題に関する本を読んだ。
examples.en: I read a book on environmental issues.

examples.ja: 契約に関しては、後ほどご連絡いたします。
examples.en: Regarding the contract, I will contact you later.

pattern: Noun + にかわって / にかわり
meaning_en: instead of / on behalf of / in place of
meaning_detailed: 〜にかわって expresses substitution or representation — doing something in place of or on behalf of someone/something else. Formal variant にかわり appears in more literary contexts. Common in formal announcements ('on behalf of the company'). The attributive form にかわる + noun also exists.
formation: Noun + にかわって (neutral) / にかわり (formal).

examples.ja: 社長にかわって、私がご挨拶いたします。
examples.en: On behalf of the president, I will give the greeting.

examples.ja: 父にかわって、弟を迎えに行った。
examples.en: I went to pick up my little brother on behalf of my father.

examples.ja: お茶にかわり、コーヒーをお出しします。
examples.en: In place of tea, we'll serve coffee.

pattern: Noun + において / における
meaning_en: in / at / regarding (formal)
meaning_detailed: 〜において is a formal / written marker meaning 'in / at' a place, time, or domain. It is a literary equivalent of で for locations and some abstract domains. Very common in academic writing, business documents, speeches, and titles. The attributive form における + noun is especially productive in academic titles.
formation: Noun + において (adverbially). Noun + における + noun (attributively).

examples.ja: 会議において、この問題について話し合った。
examples.en: At the meeting, we discussed this issue.

examples.ja: 現代社会においては、情報が重要だ。
examples.en: In modern society, information is important.

examples.ja: 日本における教育制度を研究している。
examples.en: I'm researching the education system in Japan.

meaning_en: targeted at / for (a specific audience)
meaning_detailed: 〜向け marks something as designed or targeted for a specific audience or group — 'for X', 'targeted at X'. Common in product descriptions, audience specifications, and market segmentation. The attributive form 向けの + noun is extremely common.
formation: Noun + 向け (bare); noun + 向けに (adverbial); noun + 向けの + noun (attributive).

examples.ja: 子供向けの本を買いました。
examples.en: I bought a book for children.

examples.ja: この商品は若者向けに作られた。
examples.en: This product was made targeting young people.

examples.ja: 初心者向けの日本語クラス。
examples.en: Japanese class for beginners.

meaning_en: suitable for / naturally fitting
meaning_detailed: 〜向き expresses inherent suitability or natural fit — 'well-suited for X'. Distinct from 向け, which is about intentional targeting. 向き describes a natural or inherent characteristic that makes something appropriate for a particular use or group. Common in describing personality, weather, food, and lifestyle fits.
formation: Noun + 向きの + noun (attributive); noun + 向き (predicate).

examples.ja: この仕事は彼女向きだ。
examples.en: This job is suited to her.

examples.ja: 南向きの部屋は明るい。
examples.en: South-facing rooms are bright.

examples.ja: 彼は先生向きの性格だ。
examples.en: He has a personality suited to being a teacher.

pattern: Noun / number + 切り / きり
meaning_en: only / exclusively / just
meaning_detailed: 〜きり / 〜切り expresses exclusivity or limitation — 'only', 'just'. It combines with numbers, counters, or nouns to say 'only X (and nothing else)'. More emphatic than だけ in some contexts. Also appears in expressions like 二人きり ('just the two of us') implying intimacy or exclusivity.
formation: Noun / Number + counter + きり (or 切り).

examples.ja: 二人きりで話したい。
examples.en: I want to talk just the two of us.

examples.ja: 彼は一人きりで生きている。
examples.en: He lives all alone.

examples.ja: これっきりで最後にする。
examples.en: I'll make this the last time.

meaning_en: since last doing X, (haven't done Y) / only doing X and no more
meaning_detailed: 〜たきり expresses that after doing X, nothing further has been done — often with a negative continuation clause. It implies an interruption or a state that has persisted since the past event. Common for describing situations that have not changed since a specific past moment. Distinct from the simple きり (exclusivity).
formation: V-た + きり + negative / no-change clause.

examples.ja: 昨日家を出たきり、まだ帰ってこない。
examples.en: He left the house yesterday and still hasn't come back.

examples.ja: 卒業したきり、彼と会っていない。
examples.en: I haven't seen him since graduating.

examples.ja: その本を借りたきり、返していない。
examples.en: I borrowed the book and haven't returned it.

meaning_en: not only X but also Y
meaning_detailed: 〜ばかりか is an additive construction meaning 'not only X, but also Y'. The Y clause usually extends the X claim, often to a more surprising or emphatic level. More formal than the casual 〜だけでなく. Common in emphatic or praiseworthy / critical descriptions. The shorter variant 〜どころか has a related but distinct use (far from X, actually Y).
formation: V plain / i-adj + ばかりか; na-adj + な + ばかりか; noun + ばかりか.

examples.ja: 彼は英語ばかりか、フランス語も話せる。
examples.en: He can speak not only English but also French.

examples.ja: 雨が降るばかりか、雷も鳴り始めた。
examples.en: Not only was it raining, but thunder also began.

examples.ja: 彼女は頭がいいばかりか、美人だ。
examples.en: She is not only smart but also beautiful.

pattern: Noun / plain form + と言えば
meaning_en: speaking of / when it comes to
meaning_detailed: 〜と言えば introduces a topic by taking the previous utterance as a jumping-off point — 'speaking of X'. Used to shift or extend a topic naturally in conversation. Distinct from 〜というと (similar, sometimes interchangeable, slightly more reflective) and from the fixed 〜といったら (emphatic 'when it comes to X').
formation: Noun / plain form + と言えば.

examples.ja: 日本の食べ物と言えば、やっぱり寿司だろう。
examples.en: Speaking of Japanese food, it's got to be sushi, right?

examples.ja: 夏と言えば、花火大会だ。
examples.en: When it comes to summer, it's fireworks festivals.

examples.ja: 田中さんと言えば、最近見かけないね。
examples.en: Speaking of Mr. Tanaka, I haven't seen him around lately.

meaning_en: although I say / although we call it
meaning_detailed: 〜と言っても qualifies a previous statement — 'although I say / call it X, (the reality is more modest / different from what you might think)'. It hedges an expectation by clarifying that the X claim is technically true but less grand than it might sound. Common in honest self-description and explanation.
formation: Plain-form clause / noun + と言っても.

examples.ja: 日本語を勉強していると言っても、まだ初心者です。
examples.en: Although I say I'm studying Japanese, I'm still a beginner.

examples.ja: 社長と言っても、小さな会社です。
examples.en: Although I'm called 'president', it's a small company.

examples.ja: 料理と言っても、簡単なものしか作れない。
examples.en: Although I say 'cooking', I can only make simple things.

meaning_en: on the other hand / while at the same time
meaning_detailed: 〜一方で presents a contrast or parallel between two aspects, situations, or groups — 'on the one hand X, on the other Y'. The two clauses often describe complementary or contrasting facets of the same broader topic. Formal / neutral register, common in essays and balanced discussions.
formation: V plain / i-adj + 一方で; na-adj + な / である + 一方で; noun + である + 一方で.

examples.ja: 彼は優しい一方で、厳しいところもある。
examples.en: He's kind, but on the other hand, he has a strict side.

examples.ja: 都市が発展する一方で、環境問題も深刻になる。
examples.en: While cities develop, environmental problems also become serious.

examples.ja: 仕事が忙しい一方で、家族との時間も大切にしている。
examples.en: While work is busy, I also value family time.

meaning_en: considering / for (an X), (relatively) Y
meaning_detailed: 〜わりに(は) expresses that something is unexpected or disproportionate to a given standard — 'considering X, Y is unexpected / more (or less) than you'd think'. The comparison is relative to the X premise, and the main clause often describes something surprising in either direction. More neutral in tone than のに (contrast with frustration).
formation: V plain / i-adj + わりに(は); na-adj + な + わりに(は); noun + の + わりに(は).

examples.ja: このレストランは値段のわりにおいしい。
examples.en: For the price, this restaurant is (surprisingly) delicious.

examples.ja: 彼は若いわりに、落ち着いている。
examples.en: For his young age, he is very composed.

examples.ja: 勉強したわりには、点数が悪かった。
examples.en: Considering how much I studied, my score was bad.

pattern: V-て form / i-adj 〜くて / na-adj で + たまらない
meaning_en: unbearably / can't stand how
meaning_detailed: 〜てたまらない expresses that a feeling, sensation, or desire is overwhelming — 'unbearably X'. Common with physical sensations (hungry, cold, hot), emotional states (happy, sad, worried), and strong desires. Similar in function to 〜てしょうがない and 〜てならない (see separate entry), which are near-synonyms with slightly different nuances.
formation: V-て + たまらない; i-adj 〜くて + たまらない; na-adj + で + たまらない.

examples.ja: お腹がすいてたまらない。
examples.en: I'm unbearably hungry.

examples.ja: 今日は暑くてたまらない。
examples.en: Today is unbearably hot.

examples.ja: 新しいゲームがやりたくてたまらない。
examples.en: I can't stand how much I want to play the new game.

pattern: V-て form / i-adj 〜くて / na-adj で + ならない
meaning_en: can't help feeling / uncontrollably
meaning_detailed: 〜てならない expresses that the speaker can't help feeling a certain way — a feeling or sensation that arises uncontrollably and can't be suppressed. Close in meaning to 〜てたまらない but typically used for emotional states and impressions rather than physical sensations. Formal / slightly literary.
formation: V-て + ならない; i-adj 〜くて + ならない; na-adj + で + ならない.

examples.ja: 彼のことが気になってならない。
examples.en: I can't stop thinking about him.

examples.ja: 試験の結果が心配でならない。
examples.en: I can't help worrying about the exam results.

examples.ja: 彼女が帰ってこないのが不思議でならない。
examples.en: I can't help but find it strange that she's not coming back.

pattern: Noun + 中 (ちゅう / じゅう)
meaning_en: during / in the middle of / throughout
meaning_detailed: 〜中 is a suffix with two related readings and meanings: (1) ちゅう = 'during / in the middle of (an ongoing activity)' — 勉強中 ('while studying'); (2) じゅう = 'throughout / for the entire duration' — 一日中 ('all day long'), 世界中 ('throughout the world'). The reading is determined by the base noun and usage — both are common.
formation: Noun + 中 (reading varies: ちゅう for ongoing, じゅう for throughout).

examples.ja: 今、会議中です。
examples.en: I'm in a meeting right now.

examples.ja: 一日中、雨が降っていた。
examples.en: It was raining all day long.

examples.ja: 日本中を旅行したい。
examples.en: I want to travel throughout Japan.

meaning_en: continue doing / keep doing
meaning_detailed: 〜続ける is an auxiliary verb meaning 'continue doing X' — attached to the ます-stem to express persistence or continuation of an action. Often indicates sustained effort or determination. The past form 続けた expresses completion of a long-term action, and 続けている expresses current continuation.
formation: V ます-stem + 続ける (conjugates as an ichidan verb: 続けます, 続けた, 続けている).

examples.ja: 雨が降り続けている。
examples.en: It keeps raining.

examples.ja: 10年間、日本語を勉強し続けている。
examples.en: I have been studying Japanese continuously for 10 years.

examples.ja: 諦めずに走り続けた。
examples.en: I kept running without giving up.

meaning_en: redo / do (X) over again
meaning_detailed: 〜直す is an auxiliary verb meaning 'do X again / redo X' — typically used to fix, improve, or restart an action. Common for revising, rewriting, reconsidering, rebuilding. Attaches to the ます-stem of the base verb and conjugates as a godan verb.
formation: V ます-stem + 直す (conjugates as godan: 直します, 直した, 直して).

examples.ja: レポートを書き直した。
examples.en: I rewrote the report.

examples.ja: 計画を立て直す必要がある。
examples.en: We need to redo the plan.

examples.ja: もう一度考え直してください。
examples.en: Please reconsider (think it over again).

meaning_en: suddenly start (doing X) / begin abruptly
meaning_detailed: 〜出す is an auxiliary verb expressing a sudden or unplanned start of an action — 'suddenly X', 'burst into X'. Distinct from 〜始める (planned / deliberate start). Often used with emotional or spontaneous verbs: 泣き出す ('burst into tears'), 笑い出す ('burst out laughing'), 走り出す ('suddenly start running'), 降り出す ('start raining').
formation: V ます-stem + 出す (conjugates as godan: 出します, 出した, 出して).

examples.ja: 急に雨が降り出した。
examples.en: It suddenly started raining.

examples.ja: 赤ちゃんが泣き出した。
examples.en: The baby burst into tears.

examples.ja: 彼は突然走り出した。
examples.en: He suddenly started running.

meaning_en: in the middle of / right in the midst of
meaning_detailed: 〜最中 (さいちゅう) expresses that an action or event is at its peak or most-intense moment — 'right in the middle of'. Often used for interruptions: 'in the middle of X, Y happened'. Distinct from 〜ているところ ('in the middle of doing') in that 最中 emphasizes the peak or core of the activity.
formation: Noun + の + 最中(に); V 〜ている + 最中(に).

examples.ja: 食事の最中に電話が鳴った。
examples.en: The phone rang right in the middle of the meal.

examples.ja: 会議の最中に、社長が入ってきた。
examples.en: In the middle of the meeting, the president walked in.

examples.ja: 試験の最中、集中できなかった。
examples.en: Right in the middle of the exam, I couldn't concentrate.

pattern: Plain form + もの / もん
meaning_en: because / since (emotional or justifying)
meaning_detailed: 〜もの / 〜もん used at the end of a sentence or before a main clause gives a reason with an emotional or justifying flavor — 'because, you know' / 'but I did it because...'. Common in casual speech, especially when the speaker is defending, excusing, or emotionally explaining their actions. もん is the more casual contracted form.
formation: Plain-form clause + もの / もん; often at sentence end after a main clause.

examples.ja: 行きたくない。だって、疲れているもの。
examples.en: I don't want to go. Because I'm tired, that's why.

examples.ja: 寒いんだもの、コートを着るよ。
examples.en: It's cold, so I'll wear a coat.

examples.ja: 忙しいんだもの、遊べないよ。
examples.en: I'm busy, so I can't play.

meaning_en: (it's) because / that's why (casual whining)
meaning_detailed: 〜んだもん is the casual contracted form of 〜ものだから, used to give an emotionally-charged reason or excuse — 'because, I'm telling you' / 'that's why (don't blame me)'. Very common in casual speech, sometimes with a whining or defensive nuance, especially among younger speakers and in emotional contexts.
formation: V plain / i-adj + んだもん; na-adj + な + んだもん; noun + な + んだもん.

examples.ja: 疲れたんだもん、もう寝るよ。
examples.en: I'm tired, so I'm going to bed.

examples.ja: 知らなかったんだもん、仕方ないでしょ。
examples.en: I didn't know — it can't be helped.

examples.ja: だって、好きなんだもん。
examples.en: But it's because I like it.

meaning_en: without doing / instead of doing
meaning_detailed: 〜ないで is the casual equivalent of 〜ずに, expressing 'without doing X' or 'instead of doing X'. Formed from the negative ない plus the て-form connector で. Common in both casual and neutral speech. Distinct from the polite 〜ないでください (don't do) which is already in the dataset at N5.
formation: V ない-form (without dropping い) + で: 食べないで, 行かないで, 言わないで.

examples.ja: 朝ごはんを食べないで、学校へ行った。
examples.en: I went to school without eating breakfast.

examples.ja: 何も言わないで出ていった。
examples.en: He left without saying anything.

examples.ja: 勉強しないで、遊んでいた。
examples.en: I was playing instead of studying.

pattern: Plain form + にちがいない
meaning_en: must be / certainly / no doubt
meaning_detailed: 〜にちがいない expresses the speaker's strong conviction — 'it must be X', 'there's no doubt that X'. Stronger than 〜はず (expectation) and 〜だろう (conjecture). The speaker is making a confident judgment, usually based on available evidence. More formal than 〜にきまっている (which is slightly more casual and emphatic).
formation: V plain / i-adj + にちがいない; na-adj / noun + にちがいない (no な / だ before).

examples.ja: 彼が犯人にちがいない。
examples.en: He must be the culprit.

examples.ja: この問題は難しいにちがいない。
examples.en: This problem must be difficult.

examples.ja: 忘れてしまったにちがいない。
examples.en: He must have forgotten.

pattern: Verb plain non-past + (より)ほか(は)ない
meaning_en: have no choice but to / there's no option except
meaning_detailed: 〜(より)ほかない expresses that there is no alternative to doing X — 'there's no choice but to X'. More formal than the casual しかない. The より is often dropped in modern usage. A resignation-flavored construction, common when acknowledging an unavoidable action.
formation: V plain non-past + ほかない / よりほかない / よりほかはない.

examples.ja: こうなっては、諦めるほかない。
examples.en: Now that it's come to this, there's no choice but to give up.

examples.ja: 電車が止まったので、歩いて帰るよりほかない。
examples.en: The train stopped, so there's no choice but to walk home.

examples.ja: 自分で解決するほかない。
examples.en: There's no choice but to solve it myself.

pattern: V plain non-past + くらいなら
meaning_en: rather than / if it comes to X, I'd rather Y
meaning_detailed: 〜くらいなら compares a hypothetical undesirable X with an alternative Y, where Y is preferable — 'rather than X, I'd prefer Y'. The main clause typically expresses a preferred (but often also drastic) alternative. Common in rhetorical contexts expressing strong aversion: 'I'd rather die than X'.
formation: V plain non-past + くらいなら (+ main clause preferring an alternative).

examples.ja: 謝るくらいなら、最初からしない。
examples.en: Rather than apologizing, I wouldn't do it in the first place.

examples.ja: そんな仕事をするくらいなら、辞めた方がいい。
examples.en: Rather than doing a job like that, it's better to quit.

examples.ja: 待たされるくらいなら、自分で行く。
examples.en: Rather than being made to wait, I'll go myself.

pattern: Noun + 以外(に / には / は)
meaning_en: other than / besides / except for
meaning_detailed: 〜以外 attached to a noun means 'other than X' or 'besides X'. With には, it restricts the scope: 'besides X, (there is no / only)'. It is the grammatical complement of the positive だけ (only). Very common for exclusions and exceptions.
formation: Noun + 以外 + particle (に / には / は / の); attributive form 以外の + noun.

examples.ja: 彼以外、誰もその事を知らない。
examples.en: No one besides him knows about it.

examples.ja: 日本語以外に、何語が話せますか。
examples.en: What languages can you speak other than Japanese?

examples.ja: 日曜日以外は、毎日働いている。
examples.en: I work every day except Sunday.

meaning_en: since / because (emphatic)
meaning_detailed: 〜んだから is a more emphatic form of から, combining the explanatory ん (のだ) with から. It is used to give a strong or somewhat insistent reason, often with emotional emphasis — 'since X (and you should know it)'. Common in arguments, pleas, and firm advice. The ですから form is the polite equivalent.
formation: V plain / i-adj + んだから; na-adj + な + んだから; noun + な + んだから. Polite: のですから / んですから.

examples.ja: 疲れているんだから、早く寝なさい。
examples.en: You're tired, so go to bed early.

examples.ja: 子供なんだから、大目に見てあげて。
examples.en: He's (just) a child, so be lenient with him.

examples.ja: 時間がないんだから、急いで。
examples.en: We don't have time, so hurry up.

pattern: しょうがない / しようがない (standalone)
meaning_en: it can't be helped / nothing to do about it
meaning_detailed: しょうがない (contraction of しようがない, literally 'there is no way to do') is a frequently-used expression meaning 'it can't be helped / nothing can be done about it'. Used to accept an unavoidable situation with resignation. Distinct from 〜てしょうがない (which expresses an uncontrollable feeling — see te-shou-ga-nai).
formation: しょうがない / しようがない (standalone expression).

examples.ja: 雨が降ってしまった。しょうがない。
examples.en: It started raining. It can't be helped.

examples.ja: もう遅いから、しょうがない。
examples.en: It's already late, so there's nothing to be done.

examples.ja: しょうがないから、歩いて帰る。
examples.en: Since it can't be helped, I'll walk home.

key: しょうがないしようがないstandalone
fullKey: しょうがないしようがないstandalone

pattern: V-て / i-adj 〜くて / na-adj で + しょうがない
meaning_en: can't help feeling / unbearably
meaning_detailed: 〜てしょうがない expresses an uncontrollable or unbearable feeling, very close in meaning to 〜てたまらない and 〜てしかたがない. Casual register, very common in speech. The three are near-synonyms with small register differences: しょうがない is the most casual, たまらない is neutral, しかたがない is more formal.
formation: V-て + しょうがない; i-adj 〜くて + しょうがない; na-adj + で + しょうがない.

examples.ja: 眠くてしょうがない。
examples.en: I'm unbearably sleepy.

examples.ja: 彼のことが気になってしょうがない。
examples.en: I can't stop thinking about him.

examples.ja: 暑くてしょうがない。
examples.en: It's unbearably hot.

fullKey: v-てi-adj～くてna-adjで+しょうがない

pattern: V-て / i-adj 〜くて / na-adj で + しかたがない
meaning_en: can't help feeling / unbearably (more formal)
meaning_detailed: 〜てしかたがない is a more formal variant of 〜てしょうがない, expressing an uncontrollable or unbearable feeling. しかたがない literally means 'there is no way / method', mirroring しょうがない's structure. Appropriate in writing and formal speech where しょうがない would be too casual.
formation: V-て + しかたがない; i-adj 〜くて + しかたがない; na-adj + で + しかたがない.

examples.ja: 子供のことが心配でしかたがない。
examples.en: I'm unbearably worried about my child.

examples.ja: 結果が気になってしかたがない。
examples.en: I can't help being anxious about the result.

examples.ja: 暑くてしかたがない。
examples.en: It's unbearably hot.

fullKey: v-てi-adj～くてna-adjで+しかたがない

meaning_en: how / such (a thing) as (often surprise, disdain, or dismissal)
meaning_detailed: 〜なんて is a versatile particle that can mark (1) surprise or astonishment ('how ~!'); (2) dismissal or belittling ('(things) like ~'); (3) casual quotation ('he said ~' or 'the thing called ~'). It attaches to nouns or plain-form clauses. Register is casual. Close in function to 〜などと but more common in speech.
formation: Noun / plain-form clause + なんて.

examples.ja: なんてきれいな花でしょう！
examples.en: What a beautiful flower!

examples.ja: 宿題なんて、やりたくない。
examples.en: I don't want to do something like homework.

examples.ja: 彼が来ないなんて、信じられない。
examples.en: I can't believe he's not coming.

meaning_en: things like / (dismissive) such as
meaning_detailed: 〜なんか is a casual dismissive or belittling particle — 'things like X' with a note of disdain or self-deprecation. Similar in function to なんて but more common in everyday speech. Can also express humility: 私なんか... ('someone like me...'). Often found with negative predicates.
formation: Noun + なんか.

examples.ja: 私なんか、とても出来ません。
examples.en: Someone like me can't possibly do that.

examples.ja: あんな人なんか、もう二度と会いたくない。
examples.en: I never want to see someone like that again.

examples.ja: お茶なんか、どうですか。
examples.en: How about something like tea?

pattern: Noun + をはじめ(として / とする)
meaning_en: starting with / including / such as (representative example)
meaning_detailed: 〜をはじめ introduces a prominent or representative example from a larger group — 'starting with X (and including others)'. The X is typically the most notable member of the set. Common in formal listings, introductions, and descriptions. The fuller forms をはじめとして and をはじめとする are equivalent.
formation: Noun + をはじめ (+ として); noun + をはじめとする + noun (attributive).

examples.ja: 社長をはじめ、全社員が出席した。
examples.en: Starting with the president, all employees attended.

examples.ja: 東京をはじめとする大都市では、人口が増えている。
examples.en: In big cities, starting with Tokyo, the population is increasing.

examples.ja: 先生をはじめ、生徒たちもみんな喜んだ。
examples.en: Starting with the teacher, all the students were happy.

key: をはじめとしてとする
fullKey: noun+をはじめとしてとする

pattern: Plain form + ばかりでなく
meaning_en: not only X but also Y (formal)
meaning_detailed: 〜ばかりでなく is a formal additive construction meaning 'not only X but also Y'. The Y clause extends the X claim in the same direction. More formal than 〜だけでなく, common in written and formal speech. Closely related to 〜ばかりか (also additive).
formation: V plain / i-adj + ばかりでなく; na-adj + な + ばかりでなく; noun + ばかりでなく.

examples.ja: 彼は勉強ができるばかりでなく、スポーツも得意だ。
examples.en: Not only is he good at studying, but he's also good at sports.

examples.ja: この料理は美味しいばかりでなく、健康にもいい。
examples.en: This dish is not only delicious but also good for you.

examples.ja: 雨ばかりでなく、風も強い。
examples.en: Not only is it raining, the wind is also strong.

meaning_en: not only X but also Y (neutral)
meaning_detailed: 〜だけでなく is the neutral, everyday additive construction meaning 'not only X but also Y'. It is the most commonly used of the 'not only' family, appropriate for both written and spoken Japanese. Often paired with も in the main clause for emphasis: 〜だけでなく、〜も.
formation: V plain / i-adj + だけでなく; na-adj + な + だけでなく; noun + だけでなく.

examples.ja: この本は面白いだけでなく、勉強にもなる。
examples.en: This book is not only interesting but also educational.

examples.ja: 彼女は日本語だけでなく、英語も話せる。
examples.en: She can speak not only Japanese but also English.

examples.ja: 週末だけでなく、平日も忙しい。
examples.en: Not only on weekends, but weekdays are also busy.

pattern: Noun + に比べて / に比べ
meaning_en: compared to / in comparison with
meaning_detailed: 〜に比べて (and the slightly more formal 〜に比べ) introduces a standard of comparison — 'compared to X'. The main clause describes how another item measures up against X. More explicit and formal than a simple 〜より construction. Common in statistics, descriptions of change, and formal comparisons.
formation: Noun + に比べて (adverbial); noun + に比べ (slightly more formal variant).

examples.ja: 去年に比べて、今年は暖かい。
examples.en: Compared to last year, this year is warmer.

examples.ja: 兄に比べて、弟は背が高い。
examples.en: Compared to his older brother, the younger is taller.

examples.ja: 以前に比べて、仕事が楽になった。
examples.en: Compared to before, work has become easier.

meaning_en: only after / not until
meaning_detailed: 〜て初めて expresses that the main-clause realization, action, or feeling happened for the first time only after the 〜て clause event — 'it was only after doing X that Y'. Common for insight, understanding, and first-time experiences that were triggered by a specific event. Formal / reflective register.
formation: V-て + 初めて + main clause (often past tense).

examples.ja: 日本に来て初めて、日本の文化を理解した。
examples.en: It was only after coming to Japan that I understood Japanese culture.

examples.ja: 失って初めて、その大切さが分かった。
examples.en: It was only after losing it that I realized how important it was.

examples.ja: 親になって初めて、親の気持ちが分かる。
examples.en: It's only after becoming a parent that you understand how parents feel.

meaning_en: correspond to / be equivalent to / fall on (a day)
meaning_detailed: 〜に当たる has several related senses: (1) correspond to / be equivalent to — used for counting equivalences (例えば Japanese in English); (2) fall on a specific day (今日は誕生日に当たる); (3) be one's family/relation. Formal / neutral register.
formation: Noun + に当たる (polite: にあたります).

examples.ja: 今日は父の誕生日に当たる。
examples.en: Today corresponds to my father's birthday.

examples.ja: 彼は私の叔父に当たる。
examples.en: He is my uncle (corresponds to my uncle).

examples.ja: 1ドルは約110円に当たる。
examples.en: One dollar corresponds to about 110 yen.

pattern: たとえ + V-て form + も
meaning_en: even if (hypothetical emphatic)
meaning_detailed: たとえ〜ても is an emphatic form of 〜ても, prefixing the adverb たとえ ('even / supposing') to make the hypothetical concessive stronger — 'even if (unlikely) X, Y'. It is often used when the main clause expresses firm resolve or principle against a challenging hypothetical. The basic 〜ても pattern is the base; たとえ just adds emphasis.
formation: たとえ + V-て + も; たとえ + i-adj 〜くても; たとえ + na-adj / noun + でも.

examples.ja: たとえ雨が降っても、行きます。
examples.en: Even if it rains, I'll go.

examples.ja: たとえ難しくても、諦めません。
examples.en: Even if it's difficult, I won't give up.

examples.ja: たとえお金があっても、幸せとは限らない。
examples.en: Even if you have money, you're not necessarily happy.

pattern: V-て form + ごらん(なさい)
meaning_en: try doing (warm / parental suggestion)
meaning_detailed: 〜てごらん is a casual, often parental or warm form of 'try doing X'. It overlaps with 〜てみる but carries a recommending nuance — 'give it a try, I think you'll like it'. The longer form 〜てごらんなさい is slightly more polite/instructive. Typical of parent-to-child or teacher-to-student contexts, and friends suggesting something enthusiastically.
formation: V-て + ごらん (casual); V-て + ごらんなさい (slightly more polite/parental).

examples.ja: この本を読んでごらん。面白いよ。
examples.en: Try reading this book. It's interesting.

examples.ja: やってごらんなさい。
examples.en: Go on, try it.

examples.ja: 食べてごらん、おいしいから。
examples.en: Try eating it, it's delicious.

meaning_en: feel like / have a feeling that
meaning_detailed: 〜気がする expresses an intuition, premonition, or vague feeling — less firm than 〜と思う. Used for hunches, emotional impressions, and non-evidential guesses. 気がした (past) = 'had a feeling'. 気 literally means 'spirit / mind / feeling', and the full phrase is 'there is a feeling of X'.
formation: Plain-form predicate + 気がする. For noun/na-adj: include the copula (〜だ + 気がする or 〜な + 気がする).

examples.ja: 雨が降る気がする。
examples.en: I have a feeling it's going to rain.

examples.ja: 誰かに見られている気がする。
examples.en: I feel like someone's watching me.

examples.ja: 彼は来ない気がする。
examples.en: I have a feeling he's not coming.

meaning_en: can do / is able to do
meaning_detailed: The potential form expresses ability or possibility — 'can do X'. Ichidan verbs form it by dropping る and adding られる (食べる → 食べられる). Godan verbs change the final u-row kana to the corresponding e-row kana and add る (行く → 行ける, 話す → 話せる). In modern colloquial Japanese, ら is often dropped from ichidan potential forms (食べれる instead of 食べられる) — this is called ら抜き言葉 and is widely used but grammatically nonstandard. The irregular する becomes できる, and くる becomes こられる.
formation: Ichidan: drop る, add られる. Godan: u-row → e-row + る. Irregular: する → できる, くる → こられる.

examples.ja: 日本語が話せます。
examples.en: I can speak Japanese.

examples.ja: この魚は食べられますか。
examples.en: Can you eat this fish? / Is this fish edible?

examples.ja: 早く起きられない。
examples.en: I can't get up early. (plain)

meaning_en: is done (passive); also expresses adversity / indirect affect
meaning_detailed: The passive form expresses that the subject receives an action. Ichidan verbs form it by dropping る and adding られる. Godan verbs change the u-row kana to the a-row and add れる. Note that ichidan passive and potential forms are homophones (食べられる can mean 'can eat' or 'is eaten'). Japanese also has a distinctive use of passive to express that something bad or unwanted happened to the speaker — the 'suffering passive' (私は雨に降られた — 'I got rained on').
formation: Ichidan: drop る, add られる. Godan: u-row → a-row + れる. Irregular: する → される, くる → こられる.

examples.ja: 先生に褒められました。
examples.en: I was praised by the teacher.

examples.ja: 友達に手紙を読まれました。
examples.en: My letter was read by my friend. (often with a suffering nuance)

examples.ja: ドアが開けられた。
examples.en: The door was opened. (plain)

meaning_en: make / let someone do something
meaning_detailed: The causative form expresses that the subject makes or lets someone else do an action. Ichidan verbs form it by dropping る and adding させる. Godan verbs change the u-row kana to the a-row and add せる. The distinction between 'make' (forced) and 'let' (permitted) depends on context and the particle marking the causee: を often implies force, に often implies permission.
formation: Ichidan: drop る, add させる. Godan: u-row → a-row + せる. Irregular: する → させる, くる → こさせる.

examples.ja: 先生は学生に本を読ませました。
examples.en: The teacher made/had the students read the book.

examples.ja: 子供を遊ばせました。
examples.en: I let the children play.

examples.ja: 母は弟に野菜を食べさせました。
examples.en: My mother made my little brother eat vegetables.

meaning_en: intend to / plan to ___
meaning_detailed: つもり attached after a dictionary-form verb expresses the speaker's intention or plan to do something. It is stronger than a vague thought — it implies the speaker has already decided. The negative can be either ないつもり ('intend not to') or つもりはない ('don't have any intention'). It is used primarily for first-person intention; for third-person, other constructions (と言っている) are preferred.
formation: Verb (dictionary form) + つもり(です)

examples.ja: 来年、日本に行くつもりです。
examples.en: I'm planning to go to Japan next year.

examples.ja: お酒を飲まないつもりです。
examples.en: I intend not to drink alcohol.

examples.ja: 大学を卒業したら、留学するつもりです。
examples.en: I plan to study abroad after I graduate from university.

meaning_en: I think (that) ___
meaning_detailed: と思う attached after a plain-form clause expresses the speaker's opinion or belief — 'I think that…'. The clause before と must be in plain form, not polite (食べると思う, not 食べますと思う). It is the basic way to express opinions in Japanese and is extremely common. For past belief, use と思った.
formation: Plain-form clause + と + 思う (polite: 思います)

examples.ja: 明日は雨が降ると思います。
examples.en: I think it will rain tomorrow.

examples.ja: 彼はいい人だと思う。
examples.en: I think he's a good person. (plain)

examples.ja: このレストランは高いと思います。
examples.en: I think this restaurant is expensive.

meaning_en: say that ___; be called ___
meaning_detailed: と言う has two related uses: (1) quotation — 'someone says/said that ___' — attached after a plain-form clause, and (2) naming — 'is called ___' — used to give the name of something. In the quotation use, the cited content is in plain form. The past form と言った means 'said that'. と言います is the polite form.
formation: Plain-form clause + と + 言う. For naming: 'Xという + noun' (e.g., 田中という人 — 'a person called Tanaka').

examples.ja: 彼は明日来ると言いました。
examples.en: He said he would come tomorrow.

examples.ja: 田中という人を知っていますか。
examples.en: Do you know a person called Tanaka?

examples.ja: 先生は「静かにしなさい」と言いました。
examples.en: The teacher said, 'Be quiet.'

pattern: Plain form + だろう / でしょう
meaning_en: probably / I guess / it will probably be
meaning_detailed: だろう (plain) and でしょう (polite) express the speaker's conjecture or guess about something — 'probably', 'I think', 'I guess'. They attach to the plain form of verbs, い-adjectives, and nouns/na-adjectives. でしょう is also used with rising intonation to seek the listener's agreement or confirmation ('right?').
formation: Plain-form verb/い-adj/noun + だろう (plain) or でしょう (polite). For nouns and な-adjectives, attach directly without だ: 学生でしょう, not 学生だでしょう.

examples.ja: 明日は晴れるでしょう。
examples.en: It will probably be sunny tomorrow.

examples.ja: 彼はもう帰ったでしょう。
examples.en: He's probably already gone home.

examples.ja: この仕事は大変だろう。
examples.en: This job is probably tough. (plain)

meaning_en: should be / ought to be / is expected to
meaning_detailed: はず expresses the speaker's expectation based on reasoning or evidence — 'it should be' or 'it ought to be'. Unlike かもしれない (possibility), はず implies stronger certainty; unlike べき (obligation), はず is about expectation rather than what someone should do morally. The negative はずがない means 'there's no way that' — a strong denial.
formation: Plain-form verb/adjective/noun + はず(です). For nouns and na-adjectives, use の before はず: 学生のはず, 静かなはず.

examples.ja: 彼は今日来るはずです。
examples.en: He should come today.

examples.ja: そんなはずはない。
examples.en: There's no way that can be true. (plain)

examples.ja: 荷物は明日届くはずです。
examples.en: The package should arrive tomorrow.

meaning_en: if / when ___ (general conditional)
meaning_detailed: たら is the most versatile Japanese conditional. It attaches to the た-form of a verb (or the かった form of an い-adjective, だった of a noun/na-adjective) and expresses 'if/when X happens'. It can refer to either a single future event ('if X happens' / 'when X happens') or a past event where the speaker discovered something ('when I did X, Y happened'). It's generally the safest conditional to use when learners aren't sure which of たら/ば/と/なら to pick.
formation: Verb-た + ら (食べた → 食べたら). い-adj: かった + ら (高かったら). Noun/な-adj: だった + ら (学生だったら).

examples.ja: 時間があったら、映画を見ます。
examples.en: If I have time, I'll watch a movie.

examples.ja: 家に帰ったら、手紙が来ていた。
examples.en: When I got home, a letter had come.

examples.ja: お金があったら、新しいパソコンを買いたいです。
examples.en: If I had money, I'd want to buy a new computer.

meaning_en: if ___ (general/hypothetical conditional)
meaning_detailed: The ば-conditional expresses a hypothetical 'if' — typically generic conditions or natural laws. It tends to emphasize the condition itself and is common in proverbs, mathematical statements, and generic claims. For specific contingent plans, たら is more common.
formation: Ichidan: drop る, add れば (食べる → 食べれば). Godan: u-row → e-row + ば (行く → 行けば, 飲む → 飲めば). い-adj: drop い, add ければ (高い → 高ければ). Negative: ～なければ. Irregular: する → すれば, くる → くれば.

examples.ja: 毎日勉強すれば、上手になります。
examples.en: If you study every day, you'll become skilled.

examples.ja: 安ければ買います。
examples.en: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.

examples.ja: 早く寝れば、朝元気になります。
examples.en: If you go to bed early, you'll feel good in the morning.

meaning_en: let's ___; I shall ___ (plain volitional)
meaning_detailed: The plain volitional form is the casual counterpart of ましょう. It expresses 'let's do X' or 'I shall do X'. Combined with と思う, it expresses intention ('I'm thinking of doing X'). Combined with とする, it expresses an attempt ('to try to do X' or 'to be about to do X').
formation: Ichidan: drop る, add よう (食べる → 食べよう). Godan: u-row → o-row + う (行く → 行こう, 飲む → 飲もう). Irregular: する → しよう, くる → こよう.

examples.ja: 一緒に行こう。
examples.en: Let's go together. (casual)

examples.ja: 来年、日本へ行こうと思っています。
examples.en: I'm thinking of going to Japan next year.

examples.ja: そろそろ帰ろう。
examples.en: Let's head home soon. (casual)

pattern: Verb-て + はいけない / はいけません
meaning_en: must not ___ (prohibition)
meaning_detailed: てはいけない attaches the て-form of a verb to はいけない (polite: はいけません) to express prohibition — 'must not do X'. Casual speech often contracts it to ちゃいけない or ちゃだめ. It is used for rules, warnings, and firm prohibitions.
formation: Verb-て + はいけない (polite: はいけません). Casual contraction: ちゃいけない, ちゃだめ.

examples.ja: ここでタバコを吸ってはいけません。
examples.en: You must not smoke here.

examples.ja: 図書館で話してはいけない。
examples.en: You must not talk in the library. (plain)

examples.ja: 授業中に寝てはいけません。
examples.en: You must not sleep during class.

key: はいけないはいけません
fullKey: verb-て+はいけないはいけません

pattern: Verb-て + もいい / もいいです
meaning_en: may / it's okay to ___ (permission)
meaning_detailed: てもいい attaches the て-form of a verb to もいい (polite: もいいです) to express permission or that something is acceptable — 'it's okay to do X', 'you may do X'. As a question, it asks for permission — 'may I do X?'. The more polite version is てもよろしい(ですか).
formation: Verb-て + もいい(です). More polite: てもよろしい(ですか).

examples.ja: ここに座ってもいいですか。
examples.en: May I sit here?

examples.ja: 写真を撮ってもいいです。
examples.en: You may take photos.

examples.ja: 窓を開けてもいいですか。
examples.en: May I open the window?

pattern: Verb-ない stem + なければならない
meaning_en: must / have to / need to
meaning_detailed: なければならない expresses necessity or obligation — 'must', 'have to'. It is formed from the ない-form of a verb by replacing the final い with ければならない. Many casual contractions exist: なきゃ(ならない), なくちゃ(いけない), ないといけない, etc. All of them express essentially the same meaning with varying levels of formality.
formation: Verb-ない-stem (drop い from ない-form) + なければならない. Common casual forms: なきゃ, なくちゃ, ないと.

examples.ja: 明日、早く起きなければなりません。
examples.en: I have to wake up early tomorrow.

examples.ja: 薬を飲まなきゃ。
examples.en: I gotta take my medicine. (casual)

examples.ja: レポートを今週中に出さなければなりません。
examples.en: I have to submit the report by the end of this week.

fullKey: verb-ないstem+なければならない

meaning_en: because / since ___ (softer, more objective than から)
meaning_detailed: ので expresses reason/cause similar to から, but with a softer, more objective, and often more polite feeling. It is preferred in formal requests and explanations where the speaker wants to avoid sounding pushy. The preceding clause is in plain form, but for noun and na-adjective predicates, なので is used instead of だので.
formation: Plain-form verb/い-adj + ので. Noun/な-adj + な + ので (学生なので, 静かなので).

examples.ja: 雨が降っているので、中止します。
examples.en: Since it's raining, we'll cancel.

examples.ja: 疲れているので、今日は帰ります。
examples.en: Because I'm tired, I'll go home today.

examples.ja: 電車が遅れたので、遅刻しました。
examples.en: Because the train was delayed, I was late.

pattern: Clause + が / けど / けれども
meaning_en: but / although / however
meaning_detailed: が, けど, and けれども are conjunctions meaning 'but' or 'although'. They connect two clauses with a contrastive relationship. が is slightly more formal and written; けど is casual spoken; けれども is formal. They are also often used as soft sentence openers without a strong contrastive meaning — 'well…' or 'by the way…'.
formation: Clause (plain or polite) + が / けど / けれども + clause

examples.ja: この本は難しいですが、面白いです。
examples.en: This book is difficult, but it's interesting.

examples.ja: 行きたいけど、時間がない。
examples.en: I want to go, but I don't have time. (casual)

examples.ja: 高かったけど、買ってよかったです。
examples.en: It was expensive, but I'm glad I bought it.

pattern: Plain form + んです / のです
meaning_en: explains, gives reason, or softly asserts: 'it's that ___'
meaning_detailed: んです (more formal: のです) attaches to a plain-form clause to give an explanation, soften a statement, or provide context. It frames the statement as information the speaker is sharing in response to implicit or explicit questions or context. A classic use is explaining why something is happening: 頭が痛いんです ('(it's that) my head hurts' — used to explain absence or slow reaction). For nouns and な-adjectives, use なんです (学生なんです, not 学生だんです).
formation: Plain-form verb/い-adj + んです. Noun/な-adj + な + んです (学生なんです).

examples.ja: 頭が痛いんです。
examples.en: (The thing is,) my head hurts.

examples.ja: なぜ来なかったんですか。
examples.en: Why didn't you come?

examples.ja: 実は、来月引っ越すんです。
examples.en: Actually, I'm moving next month.

meaning_en: become ___
meaning_detailed: なる means 'to become', expressing a natural or gradual change. For nouns and な-adjectives, the pattern is X + に + なる. For い-adjectives, drop い and add くなる (高い → 高くなる). The change is framed as happening on its own, as opposed to being caused by someone (for which use する).
formation: Noun/な-adj + に + なる. い-adj: drop い, add くなる.

examples.ja: 息子は医者になりました。
examples.en: My son became a doctor.

examples.ja: 寒くなってきました。
examples.en: It's gotten cold.

examples.ja: 日本語が上手になりましたね。
examples.en: Your Japanese has gotten good, hasn't it?

meaning_en: decide on / make it ___
meaning_detailed: にする expresses a decision or choice — 'I'll have X' in restaurants, 'I've decided on X' in general contexts. Literally it means 'make (it) into X' and is the active-voice counterpart to になる. It is the standard way to order food at a restaurant or make a selection.
formation: Noun + に + する

examples.ja: 私はコーヒーにします。
examples.en: I'll have coffee.

examples.ja: 明日行くことにしました。
examples.en: I've decided to go tomorrow.

examples.ja: 旅行は来月にすることにしました。
examples.en: I've decided to make the trip next month.

meaning_en: begin to ___ / start ___ing
meaning_detailed: 始める attached to a verb stem forms a compound expressing 'begin to do X'. It is an ichidan verb meaning 'to begin' in its own right, but also functions as an auxiliary when attached to another verb stem. Similar auxiliaries include 終わる ('finish'), 続ける ('continue'), 出す ('suddenly begin'), and others.
formation: Verb stem (same as ます stem) + 始める. E.g., 食べ始める ('begin to eat'), 読み始める ('begin to read').

examples.ja: 去年、日本語を勉強し始めました。
examples.en: I began studying Japanese last year.

examples.ja: 雨が降り始めた。
examples.en: It started to rain. (plain)

examples.ja: 子供たちが歌い始めました。
examples.en: The children started singing.

meaning_en: finish ___ing
meaning_detailed: 終わる attached to a verb stem forms a compound meaning 'finish doing X'. It is the completion counterpart to 始める. The standalone verb 終わる means 'to end' or 'to be over'. Note that 終える (transitive) can also be used: verb-stem + 終える.
formation: Verb stem + 終わる (or + 終える for transitive nuance).

examples.ja: 本を読み終わりました。
examples.en: I finished reading the book.

examples.ja: 宿題をやり終えた。
examples.en: I finished the homework. (plain)

examples.ja: 映画を見終わったら、電話してください。
examples.en: Please call me when you finish watching the movie.

meaning_en: easy to ___
meaning_detailed: やすい attached to a verb stem creates an い-adjective meaning 'easy to do X'. It describes the intrinsic ease of doing something, often a property of the object of the action ('this pen is easy to write with').
formation: Verb stem + やすい

examples.ja: このペンは書きやすいです。
examples.en: This pen is easy to write with.

examples.ja: 先生の説明は分かりやすい。
examples.en: The teacher's explanation is easy to understand.

examples.ja: この靴は歩きやすいです。
examples.en: These shoes are easy to walk in.

meaning_en: hard to ___ / difficult to ___
meaning_detailed: にくい attached to a verb stem creates an い-adjective meaning 'hard to do X'. It is the opposite of やすい. Note that a stronger form づらい exists, sometimes with a nuance of physical or emotional difficulty.
formation: Verb stem + にくい

examples.ja: この字は読みにくいです。
examples.en: This handwriting is hard to read.

examples.ja: この肉は食べにくい。
examples.en: This meat is hard to eat.

examples.ja: この薬は飲みにくいです。
examples.en: This medicine is hard to take.

pattern: Verb-た + り + Verb-た + り + する
meaning_en: do things like X and Y (non-exhaustive list of actions)
meaning_detailed: 〜たり〜たりする lists actions non-exhaustively — 'do things like X and Y (among others)'. Unlike the sequential 〜て form, たり does not imply any particular order or timing; it just enumerates example actions. The final する carries the tense of the whole construction. A single たり is also grammatical ('do things like X'). The pattern is one of the most common N4 constructions and is essential for describing daily routines and varied activities.
formation: V-た form + り: 食べた → 食べたり, 飲んだ → 飲んだり. List actions with 〜たり〜たりする.

examples.ja: 週末は映画を見たり、買い物をしたりします。
examples.en: On weekends, I do things like watch movies and go shopping.

examples.ja: 泣いたり笑ったりして、忙しい一日だった。
examples.en: It was a busy day with crying and laughing.

examples.ja: 休みの日は掃除したり洗濯したりする。
examples.en: On days off I do things like cleaning and laundry.

pattern: Transitive verb (他動詞) vs intransitive verb (自動詞) pairs
meaning_en: verb pairs distinguishing 'X does Y' (transitive) from 'Y happens' (intransitive)
meaning_detailed: Japanese has many verb pairs where one form is transitive (an agent acts on something) and the other is intransitive (something happens on its own). The distinction is structural: transitive verbs take を for their object; intransitive verbs take が for the thing undergoing the action. Learning the pair patterns is essential to reading comprehension and to using the 〜ている / 〜てある state-of-affairs distinction correctly.
formation: Common pairs (transitive / intransitive): 開ける/開く, 閉める/閉まる, 始める/始まる, 出す/出る, 入れる/入る, 上げる/上がる, 下げる/下がる, 見る/見える, 聞く/聞こえる, 消す/消える, 付ける/付く, 落とす/落ちる, 止める/止まる, 集める/集まる.

examples.ja: ドアを開けました。
examples.en: I opened the door. (transitive)

examples.ja: ドアが開きました。
examples.en: The door opened. (intransitive)

examples.ja: 電気を消してください。
examples.en: Please turn off the light.

pattern: Verb plain non-past + ようにする / ようにしている
meaning_en: make it so that / try to do (habitually)
meaning_detailed: 〜ようにする expresses making an effort to do something — either as a one-time decision ('I'll make sure to do X') or as an ongoing habit ('I try to do X'). The する form is the decision / resolve; the している form is the habitual effort. Negative 〜ないようにする means 'try not to do'. Distinct from ようになる ('come to be able to') and from ように-purpose ('in order to').
formation: V plain non-past + ようにする (decision / resolve) or + ようにしている (ongoing habit). Negative: V ない + ようにする (try not to).

examples.ja: 毎日運動するようにしています。
examples.en: I make it a point to exercise every day.

examples.ja: 甘いものを食べないようにしている。
examples.en: I'm trying not to eat sweets.

examples.ja: 早く寝るようにします。
examples.en: I'll try to go to bed early.

key: ようにするようにしている
fullKey: verbplainnon-past+ようにするようにしている

meaning_en: after doing X (then Y)
meaning_detailed: 〜てから expresses that the main-clause action happens after the 〜て form action is completed. It is sequential and emphasizes the 'after X' relationship between the two events. Distinct from the particle から ('because / from'), despite the shared から — here it is a compound with the て-form. Compare with 〜た後で, which more emphatically marks completion.
formation: V-て + から.

examples.ja: ご飯を食べてから、出かけます。
examples.en: I'll go out after eating.

examples.ja: 手を洗ってから、食べてください。
examples.en: Please eat after washing your hands.

examples.ja: 学校が終わってから、友達と遊びました。
examples.en: After school ended, I played with friends.

pattern: V plain non-past / noun + の + 前に
meaning_en: before doing X / before X
meaning_detailed: 〜前に marks a temporal 'before' clause. The verb in the 前に clause is ALWAYS in dictionary (plain non-past) form, regardless of whether the main clause describes a past, present, or future event — this is a common error point for learners who want to match tenses. For noun references, use noun + の + 前に.
formation: V plain non-past + 前に (always dictionary form); noun + の + 前に.

examples.ja: 寝る前に、歯を磨きます。
examples.en: Before going to bed, I brush my teeth.

examples.ja: 食事の前に、手を洗ってください。
examples.en: Please wash your hands before the meal.

examples.ja: 日本に来る前に、日本語を勉強しました。
examples.en: Before coming to Japan, I studied Japanese.

pattern: V-た form / noun + の + 後で
meaning_en: after doing X / after X
meaning_detailed: 〜後で marks a temporal 'after' clause, using the past form of the verb (Vた) even when the main clause is in the future. More emphatic about the completion of the preceding action than 〜てから. For noun references, use noun + の + 後で.
formation: V-た + 後で; noun + の + 後で.

examples.ja: ご飯を食べた後で、散歩します。
examples.en: After eating, I'll take a walk.

examples.ja: 学校の後で、図書館へ行きます。
examples.en: After school, I'll go to the library.

examples.ja: 仕事が終わった後で、飲みに行きましょう。
examples.en: After work is over, let's go drinking.

meaning_en: want someone (else) to do X
meaning_detailed: 〜てほしい expresses the speaker's desire for another person to do something. The person being asked is typically marked with に. Distinct from 〜たい (own desire to do) and from ほしい alone (want a thing). The negative form 〜ないでほしい expresses 'want someone not to do X'.
formation: V-て + ほしい; negative: V ないでほしい.

examples.ja: 私の話を聞いてほしい。
examples.en: I want you to listen to me.

examples.ja: 手伝ってほしいです。
examples.en: I want (someone) to help me.

examples.ja: 早く帰ってきてほしい。
examples.en: I want you to come home early.

pattern: Plain form + し (+ plain form + し + ...)
meaning_en: and / besides (non-exhaustive listing of reasons or facts)
meaning_detailed: 〜し lists reasons or facts non-exhaustively — 'and moreover', 'for one thing'. The listed items are not the complete set; し implies there may be more. Often paired with a concluding clause that follows from the listed reasons. It is different from the sequential て-form in that it is for reasons/facts rather than actions in sequence.
formation: Plain-form predicate + し; can chain multiple. Noun / na-adj + だ + し.

examples.ja: この部屋は広いし、静かだ。
examples.en: This room is spacious, and (also) quiet.

examples.ja: 時間もないし、お金もない。
examples.en: I have no time and no money.

examples.ja: 頭も痛いし、熱もあるし、今日は休みます。
examples.en: I have a headache, I have a fever, so I'll take the day off.

meaning_en: (someone) does a favor for me / us
meaning_detailed: 〜てくれる expresses that someone does something FOR the speaker or the speaker's in-group. The speaker benefits from the action. The honorific form 〜てくださる is used when the favor-giver is a superior. The giving-verb system (あげる / くれる / もらう) is central to Japanese expression of interpersonal kindness, and 〜てくれる captures the 'someone is kind to me' direction.
formation: V-て + くれる (polite: くれます); honorific: V-て + くださる (polite: くださいます).

examples.ja: 友達がお金を貸してくれた。
examples.en: My friend lent me money.

examples.ja: 母が弁当を作ってくれました。
examples.en: My mother made me a bento.

examples.ja: 先生が日本語を教えてくださった。
examples.en: The teacher kindly taught me Japanese.

meaning_en: I receive the favor of X doing Y / I have X do Y
meaning_detailed: 〜てもらう expresses that the speaker or in-group receives the benefit of another's action — 'I have someone do X for me'. The person performing the action takes に. The humble form 〜ていただく is used when the other party is a superior. Common as a polite request: 〜てもらえますか ('could you...?').
formation: Subject (recipient) は/が + Agent に + V-て + もらう.

examples.ja: 友達に日本語を教えてもらった。
examples.en: I had my friend teach me Japanese.

examples.ja: 医者に診てもらいました。
examples.en: I had the doctor examine me.

examples.ja: 少し待ってもらえますか。
examples.en: Could you wait a moment?

meaning_en: I do a favor for (someone outside my in-group)
meaning_detailed: 〜てあげる expresses that the speaker does something FOR someone else, usually outside the speaker's close in-group. The recipient takes に. A usage caution: saying 〜てあげる directly to the hearer can sound condescending, because it draws attention to the favor. Humble form さしあげる is used for superiors.
formation: V-て + あげる (polite: あげます); humble: V-て + さしあげる (polite: さしあげます).

examples.ja: 友達に本を貸してあげました。
examples.en: I lent a book to my friend.

examples.ja: 妹の宿題を手伝ってあげた。
examples.en: I helped my younger sister with her homework.

examples.ja: 先生に手紙を書いてさしあげる。
examples.en: I'll write a letter for my teacher.

pattern: Giver が Receiver に Object を あげる
meaning_en: to give (outward, from in-group to out-group)
meaning_detailed: あげる is the basic verb for 'give', used when the giver is the speaker or in-group and the receiver is outside that group. Crucially, do NOT use あげる when giving TO yourself (use くれる in that direction), and do NOT use あげる for superiors (use さしあげる or reformulate). The full giving-verb system is: あげる (outward), くれる (toward speaker), もらう (receive).
formation: Plain verb あげる (polite: あげます). Particles: Giver が / は, Receiver に, Object を.

examples.ja: 友達にプレゼントをあげました。
examples.en: I gave a present to my friend.

examples.ja: 犬にえさをあげる。
examples.en: I give food to the dog.

examples.ja: これをあなたにあげる。
examples.en: I'll give this to you.

pattern: Giver が (Receiver に) Object を くれる
meaning_en: to give (toward speaker / in-group)
meaning_detailed: くれる is the verb 'give' used when the giver is someone else and the receiver is the speaker or in-group. The receiver (often 私) is commonly implied and omitted. The honorific form くださる is used when the giver is a superior. Parallel to あげる (outward direction) but from the opposite perspective.
formation: Plain verb くれる (polite: くれます); honorific: くださる (polite: くださいます — irregular, note the final います not りまする).

examples.ja: 友達が本をくれた。
examples.en: My friend gave me a book.

examples.ja: 先生がくださった本を読んでいます。
examples.en: I'm reading the book my teacher kindly gave me.

examples.ja: 妹がこのペンをくれました。
examples.en: My younger sister gave me this pen.

pattern: Receiver が Giver に / から Object を もらう
meaning_en: to receive
meaning_detailed: もらう is the verb 'receive', used from the receiver's perspective in a giving transaction. The giver takes に or から; the receiver is the subject. Humble form いただく is used when receiving from superiors. Together with あげる and くれる, もらう completes the Japanese giving-verb system — each verb takes a different perspective on the same kind of event.
formation: Plain verb もらう (polite: もらいます); humble: いただく (polite: いただきます).

examples.ja: 友達にプレゼントをもらいました。
examples.en: I received a present from my friend.

examples.ja: 先生から手紙をいただいた。
examples.en: I received a letter from the teacher.

examples.ja: 誕生日にケーキをもらった。
examples.en: I received a cake for my birthday.

pattern: お + V ます-stem + ください (or ご + Sino-Japanese noun + ください)
meaning_en: please do (very polite honorific request)
meaning_detailed: お〜ください is a very polite honorific request form, more formal than 〜てください. It is the form used in customer service announcements, public signage, and formal instructions. For native Japanese verbs, use お + ます-stem; for Sino-Japanese nouns ('suru' verbs), use ご + noun. Some verbs have fixed honorific forms that replace this pattern (e.g., 来る → お越しください).
formation: お + V ます-stem + ください (native verbs): お待ちください, お座りください. ご + Sino-Japanese noun + ください: ご注意ください, ご利用ください.

examples.ja: お待ちください。
examples.en: Please wait.

examples.ja: こちらにお座りください。
examples.en: Please sit here.

examples.ja: ご注意ください。
examples.en: Please be careful.

fullKey: お+vます-stem+くださいorご+sino-japanesenoun+ください

meaning_en: honorific use of passive form (polite way to describe superior's actions)
meaning_detailed: The 〜れる / 〜られる form (normally the passive) is also used as an honorific (尊敬語), describing the actions of a superior politely. The conjugation is identical to the passive; context determines whether it is passive or honorific — usually clear from the subject (a superior) and the non-patient nature of the action. Less formal than dedicated honorific verbs (いらっしゃる, ご覧になる) but common in business speech.
formation: Same passive conjugation: Ichidan → 〜られる; Godan → u-row → a-row + れる; Irregular する → される, くる → こられる.

examples.ja: 社長が会議に来られました。
examples.en: The president came to the meeting.

examples.ja: 先生は何と言われましたか。
examples.en: What did the teacher say?

examples.ja: 何時に帰られますか。
examples.en: What time will you go home?

meaning_en: I (think I) want to do
meaning_detailed: 〜たいと思う softens the direct 〜たい by framing it as something the speaker 'thinks'. Literally 'think I want to do X', functionally 'I'd like to do X'. Less direct and more polite than bare 〜たい. The progressive form 〜たいと思っている expresses a sustained wish ('I've been wanting to'). Commonly appears in self-introductions, plans, and polite expressions of preference.
formation: V ます-stem + たいと思う / たいと思います.

examples.ja: 日本へ行きたいと思います。
examples.en: I think I'd like to go to Japan.

examples.ja: 新しい仕事を探したいと思っている。
examples.en: I've been thinking of looking for a new job.

examples.ja: 将来、医者になりたいと思う。
examples.en: I think I want to become a doctor in the future.

meaning_en: each / per / at a rate of
meaning_detailed: 〜ずつ attaches to a number + counter to express distribution — 'X each', 'X per unit', 'X at a time'. Common for fair distribution ('one each'), gradual progress ('little by little'), and instructing groups. Functions adverbially, modifying a verb or action.
formation: Number + counter + ずつ: 一つずつ, 二人ずつ, 少しずつ, 一個ずつ.

examples.ja: 一つずつ取ってください。
examples.en: Please take one each.

examples.ja: 少しずつ食べます。
examples.en: I eat (it) little by little.

examples.ja: 二人ずつ並んでください。
examples.en: Please line up in pairs (two each).

pattern: V plain non-past + つもりだった
meaning_en: had intended to / was going to
meaning_detailed: 〜つもりだった is the past form of つもり (intention), expressing an intention held at a past moment — 'I had intended to do X'. Often implies the intention was NOT carried out, with an adversative follow-up ('I was going to, but...'). Distinct from 〜たつもり, which means 'thought I did X' (mistaken belief about having done something).
formation: V plain non-past + つもりだった / つもりでした.

examples.ja: 昨日、勉強するつもりだったけど、疲れて寝てしまった。
examples.en: I was going to study yesterday, but I was tired and fell asleep.

examples.ja: 来るつもりでしたが、都合が悪くなりました。
examples.en: I was planning to come, but something came up.

examples.ja: 朝ごはんを食べるつもりだった。
examples.en: I had intended to eat breakfast.

pattern: V plain / i-adj / noun の / na-adj な + はずだった
meaning_en: was supposed to / should have been
meaning_detailed: 〜はずだった is the past form of はず (expectation), expressing that an outcome was expected but did NOT occur. Often implies surprise, disappointment, or contradiction with reality. Commonly paired with のに or が/けど for the unexpected reality clause. Distinct from はずがない ('there's no way').
formation: V plain + はずだった; i-adj + はずだった; noun + の + はずだった; na-adj + な + はずだった.

examples.ja: 彼は今日来るはずだった。
examples.en: He was supposed to come today.

examples.ja: 試験は簡単なはずだった。
examples.en: The exam was supposed to be easy.

examples.ja: 昨日、雨が降るはずでしたが、晴れました。
examples.en: It was supposed to rain yesterday, but it was sunny.

meaning_en: even (a) / or something (casual suggestion)
meaning_detailed: Noun + でも has two related senses: (1) 'even (a) X' — expressing that even unlikely cases apply ('even a child can do it'); (2) 'or something / or the like' — used for non-specific casual suggestions ('how about tea or something?'). Distinct from sentence-initial でも ('however / but') which is a conjunction.
formation: Noun + でも.

examples.ja: 子供でもわかる。
examples.en: Even a child can understand.

examples.ja: 雨でも行きます。
examples.en: I'll go even if it rains.

examples.ja: お茶でもどうですか。
examples.en: How about some tea (or something)?

meaning_en: I humbly receive the favor of X doing Y (humble)
meaning_detailed: 〜ていただく is the humble-form version of 〜てもらう, used when the favor-doer is a superior or in formal contexts. It is essential in business and polite Japanese. The request form 〜ていただけますか ('could you kindly do X?') is very commonly used in customer service, formal requests, and polite inquiries — it is widely considered one of the softest/most polite ways to ask for something.
formation: V-て + いただく (polite: いただきます). Request form: 〜ていただけますか / 〜ていただけませんか.

examples.ja: 先生に説明していただきました。
examples.en: I had my teacher explain it (to me).

examples.ja: 少し待っていただけますか。
examples.en: Could you kindly wait a moment?

examples.ja: 教えていただいて、ありがとうございました。
examples.en: Thank you for kindly teaching me.

meaning_en: should / just need to / it'd be good if
meaning_detailed: 〜ばいい expresses advice or a sufficient condition — 'you just need to do X' or 'it would be good if X'. The question form どうすればいい is an extremely common way to ask 'what should I do?'. Softer and more suggestion-like than 〜べきだ (moral should). Distinct from 〜ばよかった, which is the past form expressing regret about an unrealized past action.
formation: V ば-form + いい / いいです. Question: どうすればいい(ですか).

examples.ja: 分からなかったら、聞けばいいです。
examples.en: If you don't understand, you can just ask.

examples.ja: どうすればいいですか。
examples.en: What should I do?

examples.ja: 早く寝ればいい。
examples.en: You just need to go to bed early.

pattern: Giver が Receiver に Object を やる
meaning_en: to give (casual / to inferiors, pets, plants)
meaning_detailed: やる is the casual, down-ward variant of あげる — used when giving to someone or something distinctly below the speaker's social position, such as pets, plants, younger siblings, or in rough masculine speech. It can sound rude if used inappropriately.
