The 〜てやる auxiliary form is also very common in casual male speech as a rougher equivalent of 〜てあげる ('I'll do it for you', sometimes with threatening or dismissive tone).
formation: Plain verb やる (polite やります). Particles: Giver が, Receiver に, Object を.

examples.ja: 毎朝、花に水をやります。
examples.en: Every morning I water the flowers.

examples.ja: 犬にえさをやった。
examples.en: I fed the dog.

examples.ja: 弟に宿題を手伝ってやった。
examples.en: I helped my little brother with his homework.

pattern: いらっしゃる (honorific of 行く / 来る / いる)
meaning_en: (honorific) to go / to come / to be (at a place)
meaning_detailed: いらっしゃる is a dedicated honorific (尊敬語) verb that replaces all three of 行く (go), 来る (come), and いる (be at a place) when describing a superior's actions politely. It conjugates as a godan verb with one irregularity: the polite form is いらっしゃいます (not いらっしゃります). Common in customer service: いらっしゃいませ ('welcome' — literally 'please come/be').
formation: Plain: いらっしゃる. Polite: いらっしゃいます (note irregular — い dropped before ます). Te-form: いらっしゃって. Imperative: いらっしゃい.

examples.ja: 先生は今、学校にいらっしゃいます。
examples.en: The teacher is at the school now.

examples.ja: 明日、お客様がいらっしゃいます。
examples.en: A guest will come tomorrow.

examples.ja: いらっしゃいませ。
examples.en: Welcome. (shop greeting)

key: いらっしゃるhonorificof行く来るいる
fullKey: いらっしゃるhonorificof行く来るいる

pattern: おっしゃる (honorific of 言う)
meaning_en: (honorific) to say
meaning_detailed: おっしゃる is the dedicated honorific (尊敬語) verb replacing 言う when describing a superior's speech politely. Like いらっしゃる, it has an irregular polite form: おっしゃいます (not おっしゃります). Common in business phrases like 'what did you say?' (何とおっしゃいましたか) and 'as you say' (おっしゃる通り).
formation: Plain: おっしゃる. Polite: おっしゃいます (irregular — い drop before ます). Te-form: おっしゃって.

examples.ja: 先生は何とおっしゃいましたか。
examples.en: What did the teacher say?

examples.ja: お客様がそうおっしゃいました。
examples.en: The customer said so.

examples.ja: おっしゃる通りです。
examples.en: It's just as you say.

pattern: ご覧になる (honorific of 見る)
meaning_en: (honorific) to see / to look at
meaning_detailed: ご覧になる is the dedicated honorific form of 見る ('see / look at / watch'). It conjugates as a regular godan verb (ご覧になります, ご覧になって). The shortened form ご覧ください ('please look') appears frequently on signs, in announcements, and in instructions. Distinct from the simple honorific 見られる, which is the passive-as-honorific construction applied to 見る.
formation: Base form: ご覧になる. Polite: ご覧になります. Request: ご覧ください ('please look'). Te-form: ご覧になって.

examples.ja: こちらの資料をご覧ください。
examples.en: Please look at this document.

examples.ja: 先生はもうその映画をご覧になりましたか。
examples.en: Has the teacher already seen that movie?

examples.ja: 画面をご覧になりながらお聞きください。
examples.en: Please listen while looking at the screen.

meaning_en: (honorific) to do
meaning_detailed: なさる is the dedicated honorific (尊敬語) verb replacing する when describing a superior's actions politely. Like the other irregular honorific verbs, it has an irregular polite form: なさいます (not なさります). Common with suru-compounds: 勉強なさる, 説明なさる. The request form なさってください is a polite way to say 'please do X', though お〜ください is more common for simple requests.
formation: Plain: なさる. Polite: なさいます (irregular). Te-form: なさって. Request: なさってください.

examples.ja: 社長は毎朝運動をなさいます。
examples.en: The company president exercises every morning.

examples.ja: お客様は何をなさいますか。
examples.en: What would you like to do, sir/madam?

examples.ja: お気をつけてお帰りなさい。
examples.en: Please take care on your way home.

pattern: 参る (humble of 行く / 来る)
meaning_en: (humble) to go / to come
meaning_detailed: 参る is the dedicated humble (謙譲語) verb replacing both 行く and 来る when describing the speaker's own movement politely, especially toward a superior or in formal contexts. Conjugates as a regular godan verb. Common in formal announcements: 'the train is coming' (電車が参ります), and in polite business phrases: 'I'll be right there' (すぐ参ります).
formation: Plain: 参る. Polite: 参ります. Te-form: 参って.

examples.ja: すぐ参ります。
examples.en: I'll come right away.

examples.ja: 東京から参りました。
examples.en: I came from Tokyo.

examples.ja: まもなく電車が参ります。
examples.en: The train is arriving shortly.

meaning_en: (humble) to say / to be called (a name)
meaning_detailed: 申す is the dedicated humble (謙譲語) verb replacing 言う for the speaker's own speech in polite contexts. The most common use is in self-introductions: 'I'm called X' (Xと申します). The more formal 申し上げる adds extra humility (お礼を申し上げます — 'I express my thanks'). Business and formal speech rely heavily on this verb.
formation: Plain: 申す. Polite: 申します. More formal: 申し上げる / 申し上げます.

examples.ja: 田中と申します。
examples.en: My name is Tanaka. (humble self-introduction)

examples.ja: 心よりお礼を申し上げます。
examples.en: I express my gratitude from the heart.

examples.ja: 先ほど申した通りです。
examples.en: It's just as I said earlier.

pattern: いただく (humble of もらう / 食べる / 飲む)
meaning_en: (humble) to receive / to eat / to drink
meaning_detailed: いただく is the humble (謙譲語) verb that covers three closely related meanings: (1) to receive, as humble of もらう; (2) to eat, as humble of 食べる; (3) to drink, as humble of 飲む. The pre-meal greeting いただきます comes from sense (2) — literally 'I humbly receive / eat'. The polite form いただきます is by far the most common form. See also the auxiliary 〜ていただく covered separately.
formation: Plain: いただく. Polite: いただきます.

examples.ja: いただきます。
examples.en: I humbly receive (this meal). (pre-meal greeting)

examples.ja: お手紙をいただきました。
examples.en: I received your letter. (humble)

examples.ja: お茶をいただけますか。
examples.en: May I have some tea?

key: いただくhumbleofもらう食べる飲む
fullKey: いただくhumbleofもらう食べる飲む

pattern: くださる (honorific of くれる)
meaning_en: (honorific) (someone superior) gives to me / us
meaning_detailed: くださる is the dedicated honorific (尊敬語) verb replacing くれる when the giver is a superior. Like other irregular honorific verbs, its polite form is irregular: くださいます (not くださります). The imperative ください ('please') is derived from this verb and is extremely common. The auxiliary 〜てくださる (honorific of 〜てくれる) describes a superior doing a favor for the speaker.
formation: Plain: くださる. Polite: くださいます (irregular). Imperative: ください.

examples.ja: 先生が本をくださいました。
examples.en: The teacher kindly gave me a book.

examples.ja: 社長がお花をくださった。
examples.en: The president (kindly) gave me flowers.

examples.ja: お手紙をくださってありがとうございます。
examples.en: Thank you for kindly sending me a letter.

pattern: Noun (or V plain) + しか + negative predicate
meaning_en: only / nothing but (negative-polarity 'only')
meaning_detailed: しか is a negative-polarity 'only' marker: it must be paired with a negative predicate to give a 'only X' meaning. It is more emphatic and more restrictive than だけ, often carrying a sense of 'only this (and nothing else)' or 'no more than X'. The main clause MUST be in the negative form even though the meaning in English is positive ('only').
formation: Noun + しか + ない / いません (negative); V plain (often potential) + しか + ない / いません.

examples.ja: お金が100円しかない。
examples.en: I only have 100 yen.

examples.ja: 日本語しか話せません。
examples.en: I can only speak Japanese.

examples.ja: 一つしか残っていない。
examples.en: There's only one left.

pattern: Noun + が + 好き / 嫌い
meaning_en: like / dislike (object takes が, not を)
meaning_detailed: In Japanese, the objects of 好き ('like') and 嫌い ('dislike') are marked with が, NOT を. This is because 好き / 嫌い are na-adjectives describing the subject's state, not transitive verbs. The full structure is [subject は / が] [object が] 好き/嫌い. 大好き ('love') and 大嫌い ('hate') are the emphatic forms.
formation: (Subject は) + Object が + 好き / 嫌い / 大好き / 大嫌い + です / だ.

examples.ja: 私は猫が好きです。
examples.en: I like cats.

examples.ja: 彼は納豆が嫌いだ。
examples.en: He dislikes natto.

examples.ja: 日本語の勉強が大好きです。
examples.en: I love studying Japanese.

meaning_en: understand (object takes が, not を)
meaning_detailed: わかる ('understand / know / be clear') takes its object with が, NOT を. This is because わかる is syntactically intransitive — 'X は Y が わかる' literally means 'as for X, Y is understandable'. The same が-marking applies to できる, 好き / 嫌い, 見える, and 聞こえる. Note that わかる is distinct from 知る ('know (a fact)'), which DOES take を.
formation: (Subject は) + Object が + わかる / わかります. Negative: わからない / わかりません.

examples.ja: 日本語がわかります。
examples.en: I understand Japanese.

examples.ja: 彼の気持ちがわからない。
examples.en: I don't understand his feelings.

examples.ja: この問題が全然わかりません。
examples.en: I don't understand this problem at all.

meaning_en: can do / is possible (object takes が, not を)
meaning_detailed: できる is the 'can do' verb that takes its object with が, not を. It can express (1) ability to do X (日本語ができる 'can do (speak) Japanese'), (2) the completion / creation of something (ご飯ができた 'the meal is ready'), or (3) possibility. It is the potential form of する and can always be substituted for the より-explicit 〜することができる pattern.
formation: (Subject は) + Object が + できる / できます. Negative: できない / できません.

examples.ja: 日本語ができますか。
examples.en: Can you speak Japanese?

examples.ja: ご飯ができました。
examples.en: The meal is ready.

examples.ja: 運転ができる。
examples.en: I can drive.

pattern: Noun + が + 聞こえる / 見える
meaning_en: is audible / is visible (spontaneous perception; object takes が)
meaning_detailed: 聞こえる ('be audible / can be heard') and 見える ('be visible / can be seen') express spontaneous perception — something reaches the observer without active effort. They take their object (the audible / visible thing) with が. Distinct from the potential forms 聞ける / 見られる, which express ability (the ability to hear/see something). Roughly: 聞こえる = 'I can hear it (it's loud enough)'; 聞ける = 'I have the ability to hear it (e.g., my ears work)'.
formation: (Subject には) + Object が + 聞こえる / 見える.

examples.ja: 遠くから音楽が聞こえる。
examples.en: I can hear music from far away.

examples.ja: ここから富士山が見えます。
examples.en: You can see Mount Fuji from here.

examples.ja: 小さい声が聞こえない。
examples.en: I can't hear the quiet voice.

meaning_en: so / therefore / that's why
meaning_detailed: だから as a sentence-initial conjunction means 'so / therefore / that's why', linking a previous statement (reason) to the current statement (conclusion). It is the standalone / sentence-initial version of the causal から. In casual speech, it can sometimes imply 'that's what I'm saying' or a slight frustration. The polite equivalent is ですから.
formation: [Previous sentence]. だから [current sentence].

examples.ja: 雨が降っています。だから、傘を持っていきます。
examples.en: It's raining. So I'll take an umbrella.

examples.ja: 疲れました。だから、今日は早く寝ます。
examples.en: I'm tired. So I'll go to bed early today.

examples.ja: だから言ったでしょう。
examples.en: That's what I told you, isn't it?

meaning_en: and then / so / as a result
meaning_detailed: それで is a sentence-initial conjunction meaning 'and then / so / as a result'. It connects a previous event or reason to a consequent event or action, but with a more narrative / sequential feel than だから. Often used to introduce the next step in a story or to prompt someone to continue ('and then?'). More neutral tone than だから.
formation: [Previous sentence]. それで [current sentence].

examples.ja: 電車が遅れました。それで、会議に遅刻しました。
examples.en: The train was delayed. As a result, I was late to the meeting.

examples.ja: 昨日は疲れていました。それで、早く寝ました。
examples.en: I was tired yesterday. So I went to bed early.

examples.ja: それで、どうしましたか。
examples.en: And then, what happened?

meaning_en: and then / after that / in addition
meaning_detailed: それから is a sentence-initial conjunction meaning 'and then / after that / in addition'. It is primarily temporal (sequential), but can also list additional items ('and another thing'). It is more purely sequential than それで (which carries a causal flavor). Common in narrating actions in order and in enumerating items.
formation: [Previous sentence]. それから [current sentence].

examples.ja: 朝ごはんを食べました。それから、学校へ行きました。
examples.en: I ate breakfast. After that, I went to school.

examples.ja: パンを買いました。それから、牛乳も買いました。
examples.en: I bought bread. And also, I bought milk.

examples.ja: 宿題をして、それから、寝ます。
examples.en: I'll do my homework, and after that, sleep.

meaning_en: but / however (formal)
meaning_detailed: しかし is a formal / written sentence-initial conjunction meaning 'but' or 'however'. It is more formal than でも (casual but) and carries a more emphatic contrastive feeling. Common in essays, news articles, and formal speech. In casual conversation でも is preferred.
formation: [Previous sentence]. しかし [current sentence].

examples.ja: 雨が降っていた。しかし、試合は行われた。
examples.en: It was raining. However, the match was held.

examples.ja: 彼は若い。しかし、経験が豊富だ。
examples.en: He is young. However, he has abundant experience.

examples.ja: 勉強した。しかし、試験に落ちた。
examples.en: I studied. But I failed the exam.

meaning_en: but / however (formal-neutral)
meaning_detailed: けれども is a more formal variant of けど ('but'), used in writing or polite spoken contexts. It can appear mid-sentence as a clausal connector (similar to が) or sentence-initially as a conjunction. Less formal than しかし but more formal than けど / けれど. The casual chain けど → けれど → けれども increases in formality.
formation: Clause + けれども + clause (mid-sentence); or sentence-initial: [Previous]. けれども, [current].

examples.ja: 雨が降っていたけれども、試合は行われた。
examples.en: Although it was raining, the match was held.

examples.ja: 高いけれども、品質はいい。
examples.en: It's expensive, but the quality is good.

examples.ja: 彼は若いけれども、しっかりしている。
examples.en: He is young, but he's very solid/reliable.

meaning_en: like X and Y / things like (non-exhaustive casual listing)
meaning_detailed: 〜とか is a casual particle for non-exhaustive listing — 'like X and Y (and others)'. It is the casual counterpart of や (which lists similar items) and も〜も (which lists together). The final とか is optional and softens the listing. Common in casual speech for giving examples without being exhaustive.
formation: Noun + とか (+ noun + とか) + main clause. Can also follow verbs in plain form: 食べるとか寝るとか.

examples.ja: スポーツとか音楽とかが好きです。
examples.en: I like things like sports and music.

examples.ja: 映画を見るとか、買い物するとかしましょう。
examples.en: Let's do things like watch a movie or go shopping.

examples.ja: りんごとかバナナとかを買いました。
examples.en: I bought things like apples and bananas.

meaning_en: (casual) that... / they said... / the thing called...
meaning_detailed: 〜って is a highly versatile casual particle with three main uses: (1) casual quotation — equivalent to と (彼は来るって言った 'he said he'll come'); (2) topic marker — emphasizing or introducing a topic (日本語って難しい 'Japanese is hard'); (3) casual という ('called') for naming (佐藤って人 'a person called Sato'). It is strictly casual and should not be used in formal writing.
formation: Plain-form clause / phrase + って.

examples.ja: 彼は明日来るって言ってた。
examples.en: He said he'll come tomorrow.

examples.ja: 日本語って難しいね。
examples.en: Japanese is hard, isn't it?

examples.ja: 佐藤って人を知ってる？
examples.en: Do you know someone called Sato?

meaning_en: even so / nonetheless / still
meaning_detailed: それでも is a sentence-initial conjunction meaning 'even so / nonetheless'. It concedes the previous statement and presents a contrasting main clause. More emphatic than でも when used at the start of a new sentence — it acknowledges the previous point but insists on the following. Common in arguments and opinion statements.
formation: [Previous sentence]. それでも [current sentence].

examples.ja: 疲れている。それでも、続けなければならない。
examples.en: I'm tired. Even so, I have to continue.

examples.ja: 失敗した。それでも、諦めない。
examples.en: I failed. Still, I won't give up.

examples.ja: 難しい。それでも、やってみる価値がある。
examples.en: It's difficult. Nonetheless, it's worth trying.

pattern: Verb-stem / い-adj stem / な-adj root + そう(だ/です)
meaning_en: looks like / seems (appearance-based judgment)
meaning_detailed: そうだ attached to a verb stem, い-adjective stem, or na-adjective root expresses a judgment based on appearance — 'it looks like', 'it seems'. The speaker is making an inference from visual or situational evidence, not reporting something they heard. This is structurally distinct from the hearsay そうだ which attaches to plain form.
formation: Verb ます-stem + そう; い-adj drop い + そう (高い → 高そう); な-adj root + そう (元気 → 元気そう). Exceptions: いい → よさそう, ない → なさそう.

examples.ja: 雨が降りそうです。
examples.en: It looks like it's going to rain.

examples.ja: このケーキはおいしそうですね。
examples.en: This cake looks delicious, doesn't it?

examples.ja: 彼は元気そうに見える。
examples.en: He looks energetic.

meaning_en: thinking of doing / half-considering
meaning_detailed: 〜ようかと思う expresses that the speaker is considering doing X, but with some hesitation or uncertainty — 'thinking of doing X / half-considering'. Less committed than 〜ようと思う (intend to do). Often used for tentative plans. Neutral / formal register.
formation: V volitional + かと思う.

examples.ja: 留学しようかと思っています。
examples.en: I'm considering studying abroad.

examples.ja: 会社を辞めようかと思っている。
examples.en: I'm thinking of quitting the company.

examples.ja: 新しいパソコンを買おうかと思う。
examples.en: I'm thinking of buying a new computer.

meaning_en: is / am / are (polite copula)
meaning_detailed: です links a subject to a predicate noun or na-adjective as the polite form of だ. It appears at the end of polite sentences and is the single most characteristic word of polite Japanese speech. です does not conjugate like a verb; tense and negation are expressed through its auxiliary forms (でした, ではありません, ではありませんでした).
formation: Noun or na-adjective + です

examples.ja: これは本です。
examples.en: This is a book.

examples.ja: 田中さんは先生です。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka is a teacher.

examples.ja: 今日は月曜日です。
examples.en: Today is Monday.

meaning_en: is / am / are (plain copula)
meaning_detailed: だ is the plain-form copula, used in casual speech, writing, and when attaching copular predicates to grammatical constructions that require the plain form (e.g., before と in quotation or before から in giving reasons). In feminine and neutral speech だ is often dropped at the end of standalone sentences.
formation: Noun or na-adjective + だ

examples.ja: これは本だ。
examples.en: This is a book. (plain)

examples.ja: 彼は学生だと思う。
examples.en: I think he's a student.

examples.ja: 明日は休みだ。
examples.en: Tomorrow is a day off. (plain)

meaning_en: was / were (polite past copula)
meaning_detailed: でした is the polite past form of the copula, used to state that something was (in the past) something. It is the past tense counterpart of です and applies to nouns and na-adjectives.
formation: Noun or na-adjective + でした

examples.ja: 昨日は日曜日でした。
examples.en: Yesterday was Sunday.

examples.ja: 先生は元気でした。
examples.en: The teacher was well.

examples.ja: あの映画はとても有名でした。
examples.en: That movie was very famous.

meaning_en: is not / am not / are not (polite negative copula)
meaning_detailed: ではありません is the polite negative form of the copula, used to deny that something is something. The contracted じゃありません is equally polite and more common in casual polite speech; じゃないです is another common variant. The plain-form equivalent is ではない or じゃない.
formation: Noun or na-adjective + ではありません

examples.ja: これはペンではありません。
examples.en: This is not a pen.

examples.ja: 彼は日本人じゃありません。
examples.en: He is not Japanese.

examples.ja: 今日は月曜日ではありません。
examples.en: Today is not Monday.

meaning_en: polite non-past verb ending
meaning_detailed: ます is the polite non-past verb ending. Every Japanese verb can be conjugated into its ます form by attaching the ます ending to the verb stem. The ます form is used in polite speech with strangers, customers, teachers, and in business contexts. It expresses both present and future tense depending on context.
formation: Ichidan verb: drop る, add ます (食べる → 食べます). Godan verb: change the final う-row kana to the corresponding い-row kana, then add ます (行く → 行きます, 話す → 話します).

examples.ja: 毎朝、コーヒーを飲みます。
examples.en: I drink coffee every morning.

examples.ja: 明日、東京へ行きます。
examples.en: I will go to Tokyo tomorrow.

examples.ja: 日本語を勉強します。
examples.en: I study Japanese.

meaning_en: polite past verb ending
meaning_detailed: ました is the polite past form of a verb, expressing that an action happened or was completed in the past. It replaces ます on the verb stem.
formation: Same verb stem as ます, then + ました instead of ます

examples.ja: 昨日、映画を見ました。
examples.en: I watched a movie yesterday.

examples.ja: 朝ごはんを食べました。
examples.en: I ate breakfast.

examples.ja: 友だちに手紙を書きました。
examples.en: I wrote a letter to my friend.

meaning_en: polite non-past negative verb ending
meaning_detailed: ません is the polite negative non-past form of a verb. It expresses that an action is not being done or will not be done.
formation: Same verb stem as ます, then + ません instead of ます

examples.ja: お酒を飲みません。
examples.en: I don't drink alcohol.

examples.ja: 今日は学校へ行きません。
examples.en: I'm not going to school today.

examples.ja: 朝ごはんを食べません。
examples.en: I don't eat breakfast.

pattern: Verb stem + ませんでした
meaning_en: polite past negative verb ending
meaning_detailed: ませんでした is the polite past negative form of a verb. It expresses that an action did not happen.
formation: Same verb stem as ます, then + ませんでした instead of ます

examples.ja: 昨日、宿題をしませんでした。
examples.en: I didn't do my homework yesterday.

examples.ja: 彼は来ませんでした。
examples.en: He didn't come.

examples.ja: 先週、一度も泳ぎませんでした。
examples.en: I didn't swim even once last week.

meaning_en: marks the topic of a sentence (pronounced 'wa')
meaning_detailed: は marks the topic of a sentence — the thing the sentence is about. The topic is typically already known to both speaker and listener, in contrast to が which introduces new or focal information. は is always written with the hiragana は but is pronounced 'wa' as a particle. Understanding the は/が distinction is one of the most important and most difficult points for new learners.
formation: Noun + は

examples.ja: 私は学生です。
examples.en: I am a student.

examples.ja: 今日は天気がいいですね。
examples.en: The weather is nice today, isn't it.

examples.ja: この本は高いです。
examples.en: This book is expensive.

meaning_en: marks the grammatical subject; introduces new information
meaning_detailed: が marks the grammatical subject of a sentence and often introduces new or focal information — the answer to a question word like 'who?' or 'what?'. It contrasts with は (the topic marker) in that は presupposes the subject is already known, while が asserts it as new or contrasts it with alternatives. が is also required with certain stative predicates (好き, 欲しい, 分かる, できる, etc.).
formation: Noun + が

examples.ja: 誰が来ましたか。
examples.en: Who came?

examples.ja: 田中さんが来ました。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka came.

examples.ja: 日本語が分かります。
examples.en: I understand Japanese.

meaning_en: marks the direct object of a transitive verb
meaning_detailed: を marks the direct object of a transitive verb — the thing that the action is done to. Despite being written with the kana を, it is pronounced the same as お. を is used only as this particle in modern Japanese; the kana appears for no other purpose.
formation: Noun + を + transitive verb

examples.ja: 本を読みます。
examples.en: I read a book.

examples.ja: 水を飲みます。
examples.en: I drink water.

examples.ja: 公園を散歩しました。
examples.en: I walked through the park.

meaning_en: marks target, destination, location of existence, or time
meaning_detailed: に has several related uses: (1) target of an action (手紙を友だちに書く), (2) destination of motion (東京に行く), (3) location where something exists with ある/いる (机の上に本がある), (4) a specific point in time (三時に会いましょう). It is one of the most commonly used particles and the correct use requires seeing many examples.
formation: Noun + に

examples.ja: 友だちに手紙を書きます。
examples.en: I write a letter to my friend.

examples.ja: 東京に行きます。
examples.en: I go to Tokyo.

examples.ja: 机の上に本があります。
examples.en: There is a book on the desk.

examples.ja: 七時に起きます。
examples.en: I wake up at seven o'clock.

meaning_en: and (exhaustive listing); with (accompanying person/thing)
meaning_detailed: と connects two or more nouns in an exhaustive 'X and Y' listing, where the list is complete. It is also used to mark the person or thing you are doing something WITH (友だちと映画を見る — 'watch a movie with a friend'). A third use, quotation, is a different grammar point.
formation: Noun + と + Noun (listing); Person + と + verb (accompaniment)

examples.ja: パンと牛乳を買いました。
examples.en: I bought bread and milk.

examples.ja: 友だちと食事をしました。
examples.en: I had a meal with a friend.

examples.ja: 母と電話で話しました。
examples.en: I talked with my mother on the phone.

meaning_en: marks possession; modifies a noun with another noun
meaning_detailed: の is the most versatile particle for linking nouns. It marks possession (私の本 — 'my book'), and more generally it connects two nouns where the first modifies or describes the second (日本語の先生 — 'Japanese language teacher', 日本の車 — 'Japanese car', 木のテーブル — 'wooden table'). It is also used to nominalize verbs, which is a separate N4 topic.
formation: Noun1 + の + Noun2 (Noun2 is the head; Noun1 modifies it)

examples.ja: これは私の本です。
examples.en: This is my book.

examples.ja: 彼は日本語の先生です。
examples.en: He is a Japanese language teacher.

examples.ja: あの赤い車は田中さんのです。
examples.en: That red car is Mr. Tanaka's.

meaning_en: marks direction of movement (pronounced 'e')
meaning_detailed: へ marks direction of movement — 'to' a place. It is very similar to に used for motion destination; in most contexts the two are interchangeable, with へ emphasizing the direction of movement slightly more than arrival. へ is always written with the kana へ but pronounced 'e' when used as a particle.
formation: Noun (place) + へ + motion verb

examples.ja: 学校へ行きます。
examples.en: I'm going to school.

examples.ja: 日本へ旅行しました。
examples.en: I traveled to Japan.

examples.ja: 友だちの家へ遊びに行きます。
examples.en: I'm going to my friend's house to hang out.

meaning_en: marks the endpoint: until / as far as
meaning_detailed: まで marks the endpoint of movement or action — 'until' a time or 'as far as' a place. Commonly paired with から to express a range. まで implies the full extent up to and including the endpoint.
formation: Noun (place or time) + まで

examples.ja: 駅まで歩きます。
examples.en: I walk to the station.

examples.ja: 夜十時まで働きました。
examples.en: I worked until ten at night.

examples.ja: 月曜日から金曜日まで学校があります。
examples.en: I have school from Monday to Friday.

meaning_en: marks a sentence as a question
meaning_detailed: か at the end of a sentence turns it into a question in polite speech. In casual speech the か is often dropped and rising intonation alone signals a question. か also appears embedded in sentences to mark indirect questions (私は知りません + 何時に来るか → 何時に来るか知りません, 'I don't know when he's coming').
formation: Statement in polite form + か

examples.ja: これは何ですか。
examples.en: What is this?

examples.ja: 日本語が分かりますか。
examples.en: Do you understand Japanese?

examples.ja: 明日、学校に来ますか。
examples.en: Are you coming to school tomorrow?

meaning_en: right? / isn't it? (seeking agreement or confirming shared knowledge)
meaning_detailed: ね at the end of a sentence signals that the speaker assumes the listener shares their view or knowledge — 'right?', 'isn't it?'. It softens a statement and invites the listener's agreement. It is a sentence-final particle and can appear after both plain and polite forms.
formation: Sentence (any form) + ね

examples.ja: 今日はいい天気ですね。
examples.en: The weather is nice today, isn't it.

examples.ja: あの映画は面白かったですね。
examples.en: That movie was interesting, wasn't it.

examples.ja: この料理はおいしいですね。
examples.en: This food is delicious, isn't it.

meaning_en: I'm telling you / emphasis; informs the listener of new information
meaning_detailed: よ at the end of a sentence emphasizes the statement and informs the listener of something the speaker believes the listener does not already know. It can feel assertive or inviting depending on tone. よ contrasts with ね: よ asserts; ね seeks agreement.
formation: Sentence (any form) + よ

examples.ja: あの店は安いですよ。
examples.en: That store is cheap, you know.

examples.ja: 電車が来ましたよ。
examples.en: The train has come (I'm telling you).

examples.ja: この本は面白いですよ。
examples.en: This book is interesting, you know.

pattern: これ / それ / あれ / どれ
meaning_en: this / that / that over there / which (pronominal demonstratives)
meaning_detailed: これ refers to something near the speaker, それ to something near the listener (or already mentioned), あれ to something far from both, and どれ asks 'which one?'. This three-way distance distinction (ko-so-a-do system) pervades Japanese demonstratives. These forms stand alone as pronouns; the parallel attributive forms この/その/あの/どの precede a noun.
formation: これ/それ/あれ/どれ + verb/copula

examples.ja: これは本です。
examples.en: This is a book.

examples.ja: それは何ですか。
examples.en: What is that (near you)?

examples.ja: あれは富士山です。
examples.en: That (over there) is Mt. Fuji.

pattern: ここ / そこ / あそこ / どこ
meaning_en: here / there / over there / where (place demonstratives)
meaning_detailed: The ko-so-a-do demonstratives for place: ここ is 'here' (where the speaker is), そこ is 'there' (where the listener is or already mentioned), あそこ is 'over there' (far from both), and どこ asks 'where?'. Note the irregular あそこ (not ああこ).
formation: ここ/そこ/あそこ/どこ + copula or particle

examples.ja: ここは学校です。
examples.en: This is a school. (here is a school)

examples.ja: トイレはどこですか。
examples.en: Where is the restroom?

examples.ja: あそこにレストランがあります。
examples.en: There's a restaurant over there.

pattern: Place に Noun が あります
meaning_en: there is / exists (for inanimate things)
meaning_detailed: あります is the polite existential verb for inanimate things (including plants, abstract concepts, and events). It is paired with います for animate things (people and animals). The thing that exists is marked with が; the place of existence is marked with に.
formation: Place + に + Thing + が + あります

examples.ja: 机の上に本があります。
examples.en: There is a book on the desk.

examples.ja: 部屋にテレビがあります。
examples.en: There's a TV in the room.

examples.ja: 何かありますか。
examples.en: Is there something?

pattern: Place に Animate が います
meaning_en: there is / exists (for animate beings: people and animals)
meaning_detailed: います is the polite existential verb for animate beings — people and animals. It parallels あります exactly in structure but is used exclusively for animates. The distinction is strict: using あります for a person is grammatically wrong and will sound jarring.
formation: Place + に + Animate + が + います

examples.ja: 庭に犬がいます。
examples.en: There is a dog in the garden.

examples.ja: 教室に学生がいます。
examples.en: There are students in the classroom.

examples.ja: あそこに猫がいます。
examples.en: There is a cat over there.

meaning_en: connecting form (basis for many compound constructions)
meaning_detailed: The て-form is one of the most important verb forms in Japanese. It does not express a tense by itself but serves as the foundation for many other grammatical constructions: requests (-てください), progressive aspect (-ています), permission (-てもいい), prohibition (-てはいけない), sequence of actions, and many more. Mastering te-form conjugation is essential because it unlocks a large portion of Japanese grammar.
formation: Ichidan: drop る, add て (食べる → 食べて). Godan: depends on ending — う/つ/る → って; ぬ/ぶ/む → んで; く → いて; ぐ → いで; す → して. Irregular: する → して, くる → きて.

examples.ja: 毎朝コーヒーを飲んで新聞を読みます。
examples.en: I drink coffee and read the newspaper every morning.

examples.ja: 学校に行って勉強します。
examples.en: I go to school and study.

examples.ja: 手を洗って食べます。
examples.en: I wash my hands and then eat.

meaning_en: be doing (progressive); be in the state of having done (resultant state)
meaning_detailed: -ています has two related uses: (1) ongoing action — 'is doing' — analogous to English progressive; and (2) resultant state — 'has done and is now in that state' — particularly for change-of-state verbs like 結婚する ('get married'), 住む ('live'), 知る ('come to know'). In the second case, 結婚しています means 'is married' (not 'is marrying'). Distinguishing these two uses is an important step in early Japanese learning.
formation: Verb-て + います

examples.ja: 今、本を読んでいます。
examples.en: I'm reading a book right now.

examples.ja: 東京に住んでいます。
examples.en: I live in Tokyo. (resultant state)

examples.ja: 田中さんは結婚しています。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka is married.

meaning_en: plain (casual) negative verb form
meaning_detailed: The ない-form is the plain-form negative of verbs, used in casual speech and as the basis for many grammatical constructions (-なければならない, -ないでください, -なくてもいい, etc.). It is the casual counterpart of ません.
formation: Ichidan: drop る, add ない (食べる → 食べない). Godan: change the final う-row kana to the a-row, add ない (行く → 行かない, 話す → 話さない). Exception: ある → ない (suppletive, no あらない). Irregular: する → しない, くる → こない.

examples.ja: 今日は学校に行かない。
examples.en: I'm not going to school today. (plain)

examples.ja: 彼は分からない。
examples.en: He doesn't understand. (plain)

examples.ja: 明日は雨が降らない。
examples.en: It won't rain tomorrow. (plain)

meaning_en: plain (casual) past verb form
meaning_detailed: The た-form is the plain-form past tense of verbs. It shares its conjugation rules with the て-form, substituting た/だ for て/で. It is also the base for several compound constructions like -たことがある (experience) and -たほうがいい (advice).
formation: Ichidan: drop る, add た (食べる → 食べた). Godan: same pattern as the て-form, with た/だ instead of て/で (行く → 行った, 話す → 話した, 飲む → 飲んだ). 行く is irregular: 行った. Irregular: する → した, くる → きた.

examples.ja: 昨日、映画を見た。
examples.en: I watched a movie yesterday. (plain)

examples.ja: もう食べた。
examples.en: I already ate. (plain)

examples.ja: 宿題を忘れた。
examples.en: I forgot my homework. (plain)

pattern: い-adjective stem + くない / くありません
meaning_en: い-adjective negative (is not ___)
meaning_detailed: い-adjectives form their negative by dropping the final い and adding くない (plain) or くありません (polite). The word いい ('good') is irregular: it uses よ- as its stem in all non-present-affirmative forms, so the negative is よくない, not いくない.
formation: Drop い, add くない (plain) or くありません (polite). いい → よくない / よくありません.

examples.ja: この本は高くないです。
examples.en: This book is not expensive.

examples.ja: 今日は寒くない。
examples.en: It's not cold today. (plain)

examples.ja: この映画は面白くありません。
examples.en: This movie is not interesting.

fullKey: い-adjectivestem+くないくありません

pattern: い-adjective stem + かった(です)
meaning_en: い-adjective past (was ___)
meaning_detailed: い-adjectives form their past tense by dropping the final い and adding かった. For politeness, です is added after (高かったです), but でした is NOT used with い-adjectives — 高いでした is a common beginner error.
formation: Drop い, add かった (plain) or かったです (polite). いい → よかった.

examples.ja: 昨日は寒かったです。
examples.en: It was cold yesterday.

examples.ja: その映画はよかった。
examples.en: That movie was good. (plain)

examples.ja: テストは難しかったです。
examples.en: The test was difficult.

meaning_en: な-adjective non-past
meaning_detailed: な-adjectives behave grammatically like nouns: they use the copula (だ plain, です polite) to form predicates. The 'な' is only added when the adjective directly modifies a noun (static-adjective attributive form). Examples: 静か, 元気, きれい, 有名.
formation: Stem + です (polite) or + だ (plain). Attributive form adds な before a following noun.

examples.ja: この部屋は静かです。
examples.en: This room is quiet.

examples.ja: 彼女は元気だ。
examples.en: She is in good spirits. (plain)

examples.ja: この町はにぎやかです。
examples.en: This town is lively.

pattern: な-adjective + ではありません / じゃない
meaning_en: な-adjective negative
meaning_detailed: な-adjectives form their negative using the copula negation: ではありません or じゃありません (polite) / ではない or じゃない (plain). Because な-adjectives grammatically pattern like nouns with copula, their negation rules follow from the copula rules.
formation: な-adjective + ではありません (polite) / ではない or じゃない (plain)

examples.ja: この部屋は静かではありません。
examples.en: This room is not quiet.

examples.ja: 彼は元気じゃない。
examples.en: He's not in good spirits. (plain)

examples.ja: あの店はにぎやかじゃありません。
examples.en: That store is not lively.

key: ではありませんじゃない
fullKey: な-adjective+ではありませんじゃない

pattern: な-adjective + でした / だった
meaning_en: な-adjective past
meaning_detailed: な-adjectives form their past tense using the past copula: でした (polite) or だった (plain). As with the nonpast, they grammatically pattern as nouns with copula.
formation: な-adjective + でした (polite) or + だった (plain)

examples.ja: その町はとても静かでした。
examples.en: That town was very quiet.

examples.ja: 部屋はきれいだった。
examples.en: The room was clean. (plain)

examples.ja: この公園は昔、有名でした。
examples.en: This park was famous long ago.

meaning_en: let's ___ (polite volitional)
meaning_detailed: ましょう attached to a verb stem expresses 'let's do X' — a polite invitation or suggestion. It is the polite counterpart of the plain volitional form (-よう/-おう). It is also used to express speaker's intention ('I will do X').
formation: Same verb stem as ます, then + ましょう instead of ます

examples.ja: 一緒に行きましょう。
examples.en: Let's go together.

examples.ja: 休みましょう。
examples.en: Let's take a break.

examples.ja: 昼ごはんを食べましょう。
examples.en: Let's eat lunch.

meaning_en: shall we ___? (invitation); shall I ___? (offer)
meaning_detailed: ましょうか is ましょう + the question marker か, literally 'shall we do?'. It expresses an invitation to do something together ('shall we?') or, with first-person subject, an offer to do something for the listener ('shall I?').
formation: Verb stem + ましょうか

examples.ja: お茶を飲みましょうか。
examples.en: Shall we have some tea?

examples.ja: 荷物を持ちましょうか。
examples.en: Shall I carry your bag?

examples.ja: 窓を開けましょうか。
examples.en: Shall I open the window?

meaning_en: want to ___ (speaker's own desire)
meaning_detailed: -たい attached to a verb stem expresses the speaker's desire to do something — 'I want to do X'. The resulting form conjugates like an い-adjective (たくない, たかった, たくなかった). In Japanese, -たい is used only for the speaker's own desire or when asking directly about the listener's desire; for third-person desire, use -たがる or phrase it as a statement with other markers.
formation: Verb stem + たい (e.g., 食べる → 食べたい, 行く → 行きたい)

examples.ja: 日本に行きたいです。
examples.en: I want to go to Japan.

examples.ja: 水が飲みたい。
examples.en: I want to drink water. (plain)

examples.ja: 新しい本を読みたいです。
examples.en: I want to read a new book.

pattern: Noun + が + ほしい(です)
meaning_en: want (a thing) — for the speaker's own desire
meaning_detailed: ほしい (often written 欲しい) is an い-adjective meaning 'want' or 'desire'. It is used with things (nouns), not actions; for actions use -たい. The wanted thing is marked with が. As with -たい, ほしい is used for the speaker's own wants (or to ask the listener directly); third-person wants use ほしがる.
formation: Noun + が + ほしい(です)

examples.ja: 新しい車がほしいです。
examples.en: I want a new car.

examples.ja: お金がほしい。
examples.en: I want money. (plain)

examples.ja: 冷たい水がほしいです。
examples.en: I want cold water.

pattern: A のほうが B より + adjective
meaning_en: A is more ___ than B (comparative)
meaning_detailed: The Japanese comparative construction uses のほうが on the more prominent item and より on the reference item. The order is flexible: both 'A のほうが B より' and 'B より A のほうが' are acceptable. The adjective describes the quality being compared.
formation: A のほうが B より + adjective (or B より A のほうが + adjective)

examples.ja: 犬のほうが猫より大きいです。
examples.en: Dogs are bigger than cats.

examples.ja: コーヒーよりお茶のほうが好きです。
examples.en: I like tea more than coffee.

examples.ja: 電車のほうがバスより速いです。
examples.en: Trains are faster than buses.

meaning_en: general-purpose counter for small things (one, two, three…)
meaning_detailed: The ～つ counter is a native Japanese counter used for most small objects, abstract items, and in cases where no more specific counter applies. It only goes from 1 to 10: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ, むっつ, ななつ, やっつ, ここのつ, とお (10 is just とお without つ). Beyond 10, one uses a Sino-Japanese counter like 個 or an item-specific counter.
formation: Japanese cardinal + つ (ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ…). For 10, use とお (just the number, no つ).

examples.ja: りんごを三つください。
examples.en: Three apples, please.

examples.ja: 質問が一つあります。
examples.en: I have one question.

examples.ja: 部屋に窓が二つあります。
examples.en: There are two windows in the room.

meaning_en: counter for people
meaning_detailed: ～人 is the counter for people. It uses Sino-Japanese numbers from 3 onward (三人, 四人, 五人…) but 1 and 2 are irregular: ひとり (一人) and ふたり (二人). 4 is よにん (not しにん, which sounds like 'dead person'). This is one of the first counters learners encounter.
formation: Sino-Japanese number + 人 (にん). Exceptions: 一人 = ひとり, 二人 = ふたり, 四人 = よにん.

examples.ja: 家族は四人です。
examples.en: There are four people in my family.

examples.ja: 二人で行きます。
examples.en: We'll go as a pair.

examples.ja: パーティーに十人来ました。
examples.en: Ten people came to the party.

pattern: 何 / 誰 / どこ / いつ / どう / どうして
meaning_en: basic interrogatives: what / who / where / when / how / why
meaning_detailed: The essential Japanese question words are 何 (なに/なん — 'what'), 誰 (だれ — 'who'), どこ ('where'), いつ ('when'), どう ('how'), and どうして or なぜ ('why'). 何 changes between なに and なん depending on the following sound: before t, d, n, or the copula だ/です, it reads as なん (何ですか = なんですか); elsewhere, なに. These question words are typically followed by が, は, or no particle depending on the sentence structure.
formation: Place the question word where the unknown information would go in the answer. End with か in polite speech.

examples.ja: これは何ですか。
examples.en: What is this?

examples.ja: 誰が来ましたか。
examples.en: Who came?

examples.ja: トイレはどこですか。
examples.en: Where is the restroom?

examples.ja: いつ日本に来ましたか。
examples.en: When did you come to Japan?

key: 何誰どこいつどうどうして
fullKey: 何誰どこいつどうどうして

meaning_en: please do not ___ (polite negative request)
meaning_detailed: ないでください is the negative counterpart of てください. It attaches でください to the ない-form of a verb and expresses 'please do not do X'.
formation: Verb-ない + でください (drop nothing from the ない-form; just append でください)

examples.ja: ここで写真を撮らないでください。
examples.en: Please do not take photos here.

examples.ja: 心配しないでください。
examples.en: Please don't worry.

examples.ja: ここで食べないでください。
examples.en: Please do not eat here.

meaning_en: X and Y (and so on) — non-exhaustive listing
meaning_detailed: や lists items non-exhaustively — 'X, Y, and so on' — implying there are other things not listed. It is often reinforced by など at the end. It contrasts with と, which lists items exhaustively.
formation: Noun + や + Noun (+ など)

examples.ja: スーパーで野菜や果物などを買いました。
examples.en: I bought vegetables, fruit, and so on at the supermarket.

examples.ja: 部屋に机やベッドがあります。
examples.en: There are a desk, a bed, and other things in the room.

examples.ja: 犬や猫がいます。
examples.en: There are dogs, cats, and so on.

meaning_en: won't you...? / would you like to...? (invitation)
meaning_detailed: 〜ませんか is formed on the polite negative verb ending ません plus the question particle か. Despite its literal 'won't you' shape, it functions as a polite invitation: 'would you like to do X with me?'. Contrast with 〜ましょうか, which is slightly more assertive ('shall we?'). Responses are typically はい or 〜ましょう for acceptance and a polite circumlocution for decline.
formation: Verb ます-stem + ませんか (the same stem used for the ます form).

examples.ja: 一緒に映画を見ませんか。
examples.en: Would you like to watch a movie together?

examples.ja: 明日、一緒に食事しませんか。
examples.en: Would you like to have a meal together tomorrow?

examples.ja: 公園に行きませんか。
examples.en: Shall we go to the park?

pattern: もう + Verb-た / ました
meaning_en: already did
meaning_detailed: もう as an adverb of time means 'already' when used with past-tense verbs. The construction expresses that an action has been completed before some reference point. Its conceptual counterpart is まだ ('still / not yet'), which for 'not yet' uses the progressive negative rather than the simple past negative.
formation: もう + V た (plain past) or V ました (polite past).

examples.ja: もう宿題をしました。
examples.en: I already did my homework.

examples.ja: もうご飯を食べました。
examples.en: I've already eaten.

examples.ja: もう読みましたか。
examples.en: Have you already read it?

pattern: まだ + Verb-ていない / まだ + Verb-ている
meaning_en: not yet / still
meaning_detailed: まだ has two related uses as a temporal adverb: (1) 'not yet' — paired with the progressive negative Vていない, expressing that an action has not been completed; (2) 'still' — paired with the progressive affirmative Vている, expressing that an action/state is ongoing. Crucially, 'not yet' uses the progressive negative, NOT the simple past negative — まだ食べていません, not まだ食べませんでした.
formation: Not yet: まだ + V ていない / まだ + V ていません. Still: まだ + V ている / まだ + V ています.

examples.ja: まだ宿題をしていません。
examples.en: I haven't done my homework yet.

examples.ja: まだ食べていません。
examples.en: I haven't eaten yet.

examples.ja: 弟はまだ寝ています。
examples.en: My little brother is still sleeping.

fullKey: まだ+verb-ていないまだ+verb-ている

pattern: V plain / i-adj / na-adj な / noun の + とき(に)
meaning_en: when / at the time of
meaning_detailed: とき creates a temporal 'when' clause that modifies a main-clause predicate. The に is optional and adds mild emphasis on timing. The verb in the とき clause can be present or past, which determines the temporal relationship to the main clause: V plain non-past + とき = 'when I do / am about to do X', V plain past + とき = 'when I did / was doing X'.
formation: V plain (non-past or past) + とき(に); i-adj + とき(に); na-adj + な + とき(に); noun + の + とき(に).

examples.ja: 子供のとき、よく公園で遊びました。
examples.en: When I was a child, I often played in the park.

examples.ja: 日本へ行ったとき、友達に会いました。
examples.en: When I went to Japan, I met a friend.

examples.ja: 暇なとき、本を読みます。
examples.en: When I'm free, I read books.

meaning_en: together with
meaning_detailed: 〜と一緒に expresses doing an action together with someone or something. The と particle marks the accompaniment partner; 一緒に is an adverb literally meaning 'together'. The full pattern 〜と一緒に is very common and is one of the standard ways to express 'with' in the sense of accompaniment. 一緒に can also stand alone without a partner (一緒に行きましょう 'let's go together').
formation: Noun + と + 一緒に + main-clause verb.

examples.ja: 友達と一緒に映画を見ました。
examples.en: I watched a movie together with a friend.

examples.ja: 家族と一緒に日本へ行きたい。
examples.en: I want to go to Japan together with my family.

examples.ja: 一緒に食事しませんか。
examples.en: Shall we eat together?

meaning_en: adverbial form of i-adjectives
meaning_detailed: The 〜く form of an i-adjective is its adverbial form — used to modify a verb or another predicate ('do X -ly'). It is the same stem used as the base for negative (〜くない) and past (〜かった) forms, so it is a foundational component of i-adjective conjugation. The irregular exception is いい → よく.
formation: Drop final い from the i-adjective, add く: 早い → 早く, 大きい → 大きく, 高い → 高く. Irregular: いい → よく.

examples.ja: 早く起きてください。
examples.en: Please wake up early.

examples.ja: 大きく書いてください。
examples.en: Please write it large.

examples.ja: よく勉強します。
examples.en: I study a lot / often.

meaning_en: te-form of i-adjectives (joining / causal)
meaning_detailed: 〜くて is the 'te-form' of i-adjectives, used to join clauses. It functions like the verb te-form: linking adjective phrases together ('X and Y') or giving a reason/cause ('X, so Y'). It is distinct from the 〜で form used for na-adjectives and nouns. Exception: いい → よくて.
formation: Drop final い, add くて: 高い → 高くて, おいしい → おいしくて, 寒い → 寒くて. Irregular: いい → よくて.

examples.ja: この本は高くて、重い。
examples.en: This book is expensive and heavy.

examples.ja: 彼女は優しくて、きれいです。
examples.en: She is kind and pretty.

examples.ja: 寒くて、外に出たくない。
examples.en: It's cold, so I don't want to go outside.

pattern: Noun + の + 上/下/中/前/後ろ/横/隣/間 + (に/で/へ)
meaning_en: location relative to a reference (above, below, inside, in front, behind, next to)
meaning_detailed: Japanese uses location nouns (位置名詞) to describe spatial relations: 上 (above), 下 (below), 中 (inside), 前 (in front of / before), 後ろ (behind), 横 (beside), 隣 (next to, same type), 間 (between). The pattern is [reference noun] の [location noun] + particle. The に particle marks the location for existence verbs (あります/います); で marks the location for action verbs.
formation: Reference noun + の + location noun + に/で/へ + verb.

examples.ja: 机の上に本があります。
examples.en: There is a book on the desk.

examples.ja: 学校の前で会いましょう。
examples.en: Let's meet in front of the school.

examples.ja: 私の家は駅の近くにあります。
examples.en: My house is near the station.

fullKey: noun+の+上下中前後ろ横隣間+にでへ

meaning_en: how many / how old
meaning_detailed: いくつ is the general 'how many' interrogative, primarily used with the generic 〜つ counter for small round objects, and also as a polite way to ask someone's age. Distinct from the specific counter-based question words (何本, 何枚, 何人, etc.) which ask about a specific category. Also used for age: おいくつですか ('how old are you?').
formation: いくつ (as standalone question word). For polite age: お + いくつ.

examples.ja: りんごはいくつありますか。
examples.en: How many apples are there?

examples.ja: おいくつですか。
examples.en: How old are you? (polite)

examples.ja: いくつ食べますか。
examples.en: How many will you eat?

meaning_en: how much (price / quantity)
meaning_detailed: いくら is the interrogative 'how much', primarily used for asking prices but also for uncountable amounts (quantity, time). The most common usage is これはいくらですか ('how much is this?'). In compound usages like いくらでも ('any amount') and いくら〜ても ('no matter how much'), it takes on broader senses.
formation: いくら + ですか (asking price/amount).

examples.ja: これはいくらですか。
examples.en: How much is this?

examples.ja: このケーキはいくらでしたか。
examples.en: How much was this cake?

examples.ja: 全部でいくらですか。
examples.en: How much is it altogether?

meaning_en: what time / when (specific clock time)
meaning_detailed: 何時 (なんじ) asks for clock time — 'what time?'. Often paired with the particle に for 'at what time'. Can combine with 何分 (なんぷん) for minutes: 何時何分 ('what time exactly'). Related question words 何曜日 (what day of the week) and 何月 (what month) follow similar patterns.
formation: 何時 (question alone); 何時 + に (at what time); 何時 + 何分.

examples.ja: 今、何時ですか。
examples.en: What time is it now?

examples.ja: 何時に会いましょうか。
examples.en: What time shall we meet?

examples.ja: 授業は何時からですか。
examples.en: What time does class start?

meaning_en: what day of the week / days of the week
meaning_detailed: 何曜日 (なんようび) asks 'what day of the week'. The days of the week follow the 曜日 pattern: 月曜日 (Monday), 火曜日 (Tuesday), 水曜日 (Wednesday), 木曜日 (Thursday), 金曜日 (Friday), 土曜日 (Saturday), 日曜日 (Sunday). Named after the sun (日), moon (月), and the five classical elements: fire (火), water (水), wood (木), metal (金), earth (土).
formation: Question: 何曜日. Each day: [element kanji] + 曜日. Time marker: 〜曜日 + に ('on [day]').

examples.ja: 今日は何曜日ですか。
examples.en: What day of the week is it today?

examples.ja: 月曜日に会議があります。
examples.en: There is a meeting on Monday.

examples.ja: 土曜日と日曜日は休みです。
examples.en: Saturday and Sunday are days off.

meaning_en: o'clock (hour counter)
meaning_detailed: 〜時 (じ) is the counter for clock hours — 'X o'clock'. Numbers 1-12 are used, but several have irregular readings: 4時 (よじ), 7時 (しちじ), 9時 (くじ). Combined with 〜分 (minutes) for specific times. Used with particle に for 'at X o'clock'.
formation: Number + 時. Irregulars: 4 → よ, 7 → しち, 9 → く.

examples.ja: 今、3時です。
examples.en: It's 3 o'clock now.

examples.ja: 9時に学校へ行きます。
examples.en: I go to school at 9 o'clock.

examples.ja: 4時の電車に乗ります。
examples.en: I'll take the 4 o'clock train.

meaning_en: minute (time / duration counter)
meaning_detailed: 〜分 (ふん / ぷん) is the counter for minutes — both clock-time minutes and duration. Reading changes between ふん (voiceless) and ぷん (voiced / geminated) depending on the preceding number. Several numbers have irregular or combined forms. Common contexts: clock time (3時10分), duration (10分), distance by time (駅から5分).
formation: Number + 分. Reading: ぷん after 1/3/4/6/8/10; ふん after 2/5/7/9. Half-hour fixed form: 半 (はん, for 30 minutes).

examples.ja: 10分待ってください。
examples.en: Please wait 10 minutes.

examples.ja: 今、3時15分です。
examples.en: It's 3:15 now.

examples.ja: 駅まで5分かかります。
examples.en: It takes 5 minutes to the station.

meaning_en: year of age (age counter)
meaning_detailed: 〜歳 (さい) is the counter for age — the number of years a person has lived. The alternate kanji 才 is commonly used, especially in casual writing. Several readings are irregular: 1歳 (いっさい), 8歳 (はっさい), 10歳 (じっさい / じゅっさい), and 20歳 (はたち, a fully irregular traditional reading for 20 years old).
formation: Number + 歳 (or 才). Irregulars: 1→いっ, 8→はっ, 10→じっ/じゅっ, 20→はたち.

examples.ja: 私は20歳です。
examples.en: I am 20 years old.

examples.ja: 弟は12歳です。
examples.en: My younger brother is 12 years old.

examples.ja: 彼は何歳ですか。
examples.en: How old is he?

meaning_en: yen (Japanese currency counter)
meaning_detailed: 〜円 (えん) is the counter for Japanese yen — the national currency. Numbers attach directly without sound changes. Used for all prices, costs, and monetary amounts. Question form: いくらですか or 何円ですか.
formation: Number + 円. No sound changes.

examples.ja: このケーキは500円です。
examples.en: This cake is 500 yen.

examples.ja: 財布に3000円あります。
examples.en: I have 3000 yen in my wallet.

examples.ja: これは1万円です。
examples.en: This is 10,000 yen.

meaning_en: counter for long, thin objects
meaning_detailed: 〜本 (ほん / ぼん / ぽん) is the counter for long, thin objects — pencils, bottles, umbrellas, trees, bananas, wire, roads, trains, phone calls, films, etc. The reading changes between ほん (voiceless), ぼん (voiced), and ぽん (geminated) depending on the preceding number. Classic example of a counter with variable readings, a distinctive feature of Japanese.
formation: Number + 本. Readings: 1ぽん, 2ほん, 3ぼん, 4ほん, 5ほん, 6ぽん, 7ほん, 8ぽん, 9ほん, 10ぽん.

examples.ja: 鉛筆を3本買いました。
examples.en: I bought 3 pencils.

examples.ja: 水を2本ください。
examples.en: Please give me 2 bottles of water.

examples.ja: 傘を何本持っていますか。
examples.en: How many umbrellas do you have?

meaning_en: counter for flat, thin objects
meaning_detailed: 〜枚 (まい) is the counter for flat, thin objects — paper, photos, tickets, plates, T-shirts, slices of bread/cheese, CDs, floor mats. Unlike 本, 枚 has no sound changes — it attaches cleanly to all numbers. One of the easiest counters for learners because of its regularity. Question form: 何枚 (なんまい).
formation: Number + 枚. No sound changes — attaches cleanly to all numbers.

examples.ja: 紙を3枚ください。
examples.en: Please give me 3 sheets of paper.

examples.ja: 切符を2枚買いました。
examples.en: I bought 2 tickets.

examples.ja: 写真を何枚撮りましたか。
examples.en: How many photos did you take?

meaning_en: every / each (time period)
meaning_detailed: 毎 (まい) is a prefix meaning 'every' that attaches to time-period nouns: 毎日 (every day), 毎週 (every week), 毎月 (every month), 毎年 (every year), 毎朝 (every morning), 毎晩 (every evening). Used adverbially to describe recurring actions — more convenient than 'いつも' (always) for specifying frequency by time unit.
formation: 毎 + time period noun: 毎日, 毎週, 毎月, 毎年, 毎朝, 毎晩, 毎時, 毎回.

examples.ja: 毎日、コーヒーを飲みます。
examples.en: I drink coffee every day.

examples.ja: 毎朝、6時に起きます。
examples.en: I get up at 6 every morning.

examples.ja: 毎週末、買い物に行きます。
examples.en: I go shopping every weekend.

meaning_en: hour (duration counter)
meaning_detailed: 〜時間 (じかん) is the counter for hours of duration — how many hours something lasts, as opposed to 〜時 which is for clock time. 3時間 means 'three hours' (duration); 3時 means '3 o'clock'. Common in durations of study, work, travel, sleep. No sound changes.
formation: Number + 時間. No sound changes.

examples.ja: 毎日、2時間勉強します。
examples.en: I study for 2 hours every day.

examples.ja: 東京まで3時間かかります。
examples.en: It takes 3 hours to Tokyo.

examples.ja: 昨日は8時間寝ました。
examples.en: I slept 8 hours yesterday.
